releases.body:
Four students to receive $5,000 scholarships recognizing leadership, advocacy, service, and community impact

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University Credit Union (UCU) is currently accepting applications for its 2027 Scholarship Program, which provides four $5,000 awards to student members who demonstrate exceptional leadership, advocacy, and community service. This annual initiative aims to alleviate the financial burden of higher education while recognizing individuals who drive positive social change within their institutions.

Interested applicants can access the official application and full eligibility requirements at ucu.org/scholarship.

"Education has the power to transform lives, strengthen communities, and open doors to new opportunities," said UCU's President and CEO, Richard Wada. "Through our scholarship program, we are supporting students who are not only striving for academic excellence but are also addressing barriers, leading with purpose, and creating a lasting impact for others."

2027 Scholarship Categories

To ensure a broad impact, the program features four distinct awards that align with the organization's commitment to service and equity:

  • Al Aubin Advocacy Scholarship: Recognizes students who have actively worked to reduce barriers for underrepresented groups in higher education.
  • Jane Permaul Women in Leadership Scholarship: Celebrates individuals who have demonstrated leadership and helped advance professional opportunities for women.
  • Norma Iadevaia Service and Leadership Scholarship: Honors students who exemplify resilience and a consistent commitment to community service.
  • Financial Advantage Scholarship: Supports students who plan to use their education to create a measurable positive impact in their local communities.

Applications are open to current student members across all levels of study, including high school, undergraduate, and graduate programs. Candidates are required to submit an essay of 500 words or less addressing the specific criteria for their selected scholarship category.

A selection committee comprising representatives from the credit union will review all submissions to identify one recipient for each category.

The deadline for electronic submission of all application materials is February 22, 2027.

UCU is a purpose-driven financial cooperative dedicated to providing a financial edge to the university community. Founded in 1951 on campus by UCLA employees, UCU focuses on member-owner participation and returns profits to its members through better loan rates, higher savings rates, and lower fees. Today, serving over 60,000 members, UCU offers a range of financial products and services, including checking accounts, loans, and insurance, while emphasizing community support and financial education. Learn more at ucu.org.

Phone: 800.UCU.4510

releases.body:
Celebrating National STEM Day on Nov. 8 by Helping Students Pursue STEM Careers

Link to B-roll video and soundbites of STEM recipients

OAKLAND, Calif., Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The PG&E Corporation Foundation (PG&E Foundation) awarded $327,500 in scholarships to dozens of students pursuing degrees in science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) at colleges and universities across California and Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) nationwide.

As communities celebrate National STEM Day on Nov. 8, the PG&E Foundation reaffirms its commitment to building tomorrow's workforce through investments in STEM education and scholarships.

This year, scholarships in the amounts of $2,500, $5,000 and $10,000 are being granted to 57 students from across Pacific Gas and Electric Company's (PG&E) service area through the program.

Since 2012, the Better Together STEM Scholarship Program has awarded nearly $8 million to accomplished students. This contribution is funded by PG&E shareholders and is not recovered through customer rates.

By investing in STEM education, the Foundation helps inspire curiosity, creativity, and innovation while empowering students to develop solutions and technologies that can make a positive impact in their hometown communities and beyond.

Scholarship recipients include Quennel Kempe of Fresno and Caden Kelly of Shingle Springs. Both students attend UC Berkeley. Kempe received a $5,000 scholarship and Kelly received a $2,500 scholarship.

"Receiving the PG&E STEM Scholarship shows me that my community believes in me. The financial assistance and encouragement give me the confidence to achieve my goals and make a greater impact in the future," said Kempe, who is studying computer science. 

"The PG&E STEM Scholarship has given me the freedom to focus fully on my education without the added stress of financial challenges. It also serves as a reminder of the values I want to carry forward, using my education to give back to my community, supporting others and helping make STEM opportunities more accessible for future generations," said Kelly who is studying electrical engineering.

Scholarships are based on academic achievement, demonstrated participation and leadership in school and community activities, and financial need. Recipients may reapply annually for up to five years.

Watch PG&E's video series of past STEM scholar recipients.

"We hope these students discover a path in science, technology, engineering, and math that not only leads to new innovations and breakthroughs but also brings them fulfillment and a sense of purpose. We are proud to support them on their journey as they pursue their higher education goals and dreams," said Carla Peterman, President, PG&E Corporation, and Chair of The PG&E Corporation Foundation Board.

Scholarship recipients must plan to enroll in full-time undergraduate study for the entire 2026-2027 academic year and pursue their first undergraduate degree at an accredited four-year institution in California. HBCU eligibility was recently added after an increasing number of applicants were admitted to historically Black colleges and universities, none of which are in California.

Employees Supporting Local Scholars

In addition to the Better Together STEM Scholarship Program, PG&E's 11 employee resource groups (ERGs) and three engineering networking groups (ENGs) award scholarships to help offset the cost of higher education. The funds are raised entirely from employee contributions through direct donations, fundraising events and the company's employee giving program known as Campaign for the Community. Since 1989, more than $6 million ERG/ENG Scholarships has been raised and awarded to thousands of our hometown students.

About PG&E

Pacific Gas and Electric Company, a subsidiary of PG&E Corporation (NYSE: PCG), is a combined natural gas and electric utility serving more than 16 million people across 70,000 square miles in Northern and Central California. For more information, visit www.pge.com/ and http://www.pge.com/about/newsroom/.

About The PG&E Corporation Foundation

The PG&E Corporation Foundation is an independent 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, separate from PG&E and sponsored by PG&E Corporation.

releases.title: Basta Marks 10 Years of Expanding Career Access for First-Generation College Students, Aims to Impact One Million Careers by 2030
releases.body:
From 40 students in New York City to more than 85,000 nationally, Basta celebrates a decade of connecting talent to opportunity alongside alumni, corporate partners, and higher education leaders.

NEW YORK, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Basta, a national nonprofit working to close the employment gap for first-generation college students, marked its tenth anniversary on October 20 with its Once-in-a-Decade Gala at Jazz at Lincoln Center's Frederick P. Rose Hall. The celebration brought together alumni, corporate and philanthropic leaders, and higher education partners to reflect on a decade of expanding career access and Basta's ambition to impact one million careers by 2030.

Founded in New York City in 2016 with just 40 students, Basta has grown into a tech-enabled nonprofit reaching more than 85,000 students across 300+ college campuses.

"For too many first-generation college students, the difference between landing a strong first job and being overlooked comes down to who they know and which doors happen to open," said Basta Founder and CEO Sheila Sarem. "Over the past decade, we've seen what becomes possible when we connect talented young people with the knowledge, networks, and opportunities they deserve. Our ambition is to extend that impact to one million careers by 2030."

That impact came to life through alumni stories shared throughout the evening. Among them was Keyshawn Wright, a 2018 Basta alum who described how mentorship and exposure to new career paths helped him navigate his first professional opportunity. Today, Wright is a director in technology program management at Morgan Stanley.

"Never underestimate the ripple effect of making a connection. When you open a door for a first-gen student, they'll run right through it," Wright told the audience.

The evening also honored Bloomberg with Basta's First Champion Award, recognizing the company as Basta's first employer partner in 2019 and celebrating a relationship that has helped shape the organization's approach to connecting first-generation talent with professional networks and career opportunities. In a special video message, Bloomberg founder and former New York City Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg reflected on the partnership, which has engaged more than 1,000 Bloomberg employees as volunteers and connected more than 500 Basta participants with Bloomberg mentors.

The celebration brought together longstanding corporate partners, including Bloomberg and BNY, alongside higher education leaders SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. and CUNY Chancellor Félix V. Matos Rodríguez, underscoring the importance of strengthening pathways between education and employment.

Hosted by NBC News Daily anchor Vicky Nguyen, the evening featured a special performance by musicians Will Butler and Sarah Neufeld, formerly of Arcade Fire.

Photos: Courtesy of Basta | Jazz at Lincoln Center's Frederick P. Rose Hall

About Basta

Basta is a national tech nonprofit closing the employment gap for first-generation college students. Combining personalized career coaching, employer connections, and AI-powered technology, Basta expands access to the knowledge, networks, and opportunities that launch strong careers. Founded in 2016, Basta has reached more than 85,000 students across 300+ college campuses nationwide.

Learn more at www.projectbasta.com

releases.body:
ATLANTA, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- UCB, a global biopharmaceutical company, today announced the opening of applications for the third annual UCB U.S. Myasthenia Gravis Scholarship™, supporting individuals impacted by myasthenia gravis (MG), including patients, caregivers, and family members pursuing higher education. To learn more about the UCB Myasthenia Gravis Scholarship or to apply online, visit www.UCBMGScholarship.com. In 2027, UCB will again award 15 scholarships. The application deadline is January 31, 2027. 

"For three years, the UCB U.S. Myasthenia Gravis Scholarship has celebrated the resilience, determination, and aspirations of people impacted by MG," said Kimberly Moran, PhD, MBA, SVP & Head, U.S. Rare Diseases, UCB. "As applications open again this year, we're proud to continue investing in the educational goals of patients, caregivers, and family members who are pursuing their dreams despite the challenges MG can bring. Supporting people beyond medicine remains a core part of our commitment to the MG community."

Since its launch, the scholarship program has helped recipients pursue a wide range of educational and professional goals, from undergraduate and graduate degrees to specialized certifications and career advancement opportunities.

A 2025 scholarship recipient and caregiver of her mother living with MG, Joleen Rockhill of Clearwater, Florida, exemplifies the lasting impact of the UCB U.S. Myasthenia Gravis Scholarship. Joleen recently earned her doctorate in nursing practice from Galen College of Nursing, achieving a significant milestone in her academic journey.

"As I near the end of this academic journey, I also want to take a moment to thank UCB for the support and financial assistance I've received throughout this program. I honestly don't know if I would have been able to complete my doctoral degree without it," said Joleen. "This experience has helped me grow tremendously, not only professionally, but also as a volunteer with the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America and as an advocate for the MG community."

Today, Ms. Rockhill is applying her education and lived experience to improve care for people living with MG. She is developing continuing education courses designed to help first responders and nurses better recognize MG exacerbations, understand oxygen-related considerations for MG patients, and identify medications that may be safe or unsafe for this population. She is also developing a high-fidelity simulation experience designed to help patients and caregivers build confidence in recognizing urgent symptoms, navigating emergency situations, and preparing for hospitalization. While the experience may be featured at future patient conferences, Ms. Rockhill's long-term vision is to expand its reach through educational programs, patient and caregiver initiatives, and potentially virtual and technology-enabled formats to make the experience accessible to a broader community of people affected by MG and other rare diseases.

"When my mother was first diagnosed, an experience like this would have meant so much to me," said Joleen. "My hope is to create opportunities for patients and caregivers to safely work through urgent or emergent scenarios before they encounter them in real life. Over time, I would love to see this evolve beyond a single event and become available through additional educational programs and potentially even computer-based or virtual experiences for families who may not be able to travel. Navigating a new and unpredictable disease can be overwhelming, and I know that firsthand. Even as an experienced critical care nurse, there were times when I felt unprepared to manage the more unstable aspects of my mother's MG. If this project can help reduce some of that fear while giving patients and caregivers greater confidence in recognizing and responding to concerning situations, I believe it could have a meaningful impact."

Visit the UCB MG Scholarship website to learn more about the program, hear from past recipients, and submit an application.

releases.body:
The two-year online college's new concentration, embedded in its Associate of Arts in Business Administration, prepares students for marketing and brand strategy careers built on the data, platforms, and AI tools companies now use to reach customers.

NEW YORK, November 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Campus, the two-year online college built for a generation of learners frustrated by the cost and pace of higher education, today announced the launch of its Associate of Arts in Business Administration (AABA) with a Concentration in Digital Marketing and the Creator Economy. The concentration is designed to prepare students for entry-level roles in digital marketing, brand strategy, and content-driven business functions, or to transfer into related bachelor's degree programs.

"Marketing is undergoing a real shift. Brands increasingly operate like media companies, building audiences through content that is authentic and grabbing," said Todd Fitch, Program Director for Campus' Associate of Arts in Business Administration program. "But, it's also become a technical job. Our students learn to pair original ideas with the analytical and production skills that bring those ideas to life."

Goldman Sachs Research projects the creator economy's total addressable market could roughly double from $250 billion to $480 billion by 2027, driven largely by brand investment in influencer marketing and platform advertising. Meanwhile, LinkedIn's 2026 analysis of the fastest-growing marketing skills ranks performance analysis and AI literacy as the top two capabilities employers are hiring for — skills taught in Campus's new program.

Timm Chiusano, a former advertising executive at ABC, ESPN, and Spectrum, has joined Campus as a visiting professor for the program and has helped shape the concentration's curriculum. A full-time creator himself with more than 1 million followers, he brings expertise building audiences and brands on both sides of the media industry. He will deliver guest lectures when the concentration launches in January 2027.

The concentration consists of five courses woven into students' standard business course sequence. Students will build knowledge across brand strategy, platform dynamics, and marketing analytics, culminating in a capstone in either creator-brand strategy and content or marketing analytics.

Students will also learn to use AI as part of modern ideation, production, research, and workflow processes without using it as a substitute for the originality and creative judgment that digital marketing demands. Along the way, students build a portfolio that demonstrates how they research audiences, develop brands, create content, plan campaigns, and use performance data to improve their work.

"I didn't take the traditional path. I went from no college degree to Fortune 100 executive to full-time creator, and along the way realized I really love helping people figure out how to thrive at work," said Chiusano, whose viral content focuses on practical, motivational advice for Gen Z. "I'm honored to apply my real-life experience, and help the next generation of media innovators build careers they love, without drowning in debt to make that happen."

The first college built in the AI era, Campus is backed by entrepreneurs and investors including Sam Altman, Shaquille O'Neal, General Catalyst, Founders Fund, and 8VC, and is led by a board of respected former college presidents including John Wilson of Morehouse College and Gail Mellow of LaGuardia Community College. Campus delivers live, online classes taught by faculty who also teach at top colleges like UCLA, Stanford, and Howard. Campus' unique approach is grounded in a pioneering tech platform and a heavily-researched student success model proven to double two-year college graduation rates. Campus provides students with dedicated advisors, on-demand tutoring, and personalized coaching. Upon completion, students take skills learned in the program into the workforce or transfer to a growing number of four-year institution transfer partners.

Learn more about Campus' Digital Marketing and the Creator Economy concentration at http://campus.edu/business-degree-digital-marketing-concentration.

Campus delivers live, online classes taught by professors who also teach at leading universities like Stanford, and Howard University. The college's unique approach is grounded in a pioneering technology platform and a heavily-researched student success model that offers students dedicated advisors and on-demand tutoring and coaching to ensure their academic access. releases.body:
• 71% of college students surveyed say their school prioritizes mental health

• 49% of administrators surveyed say their institutions conduct regular wellness screenings

NEW YORK, Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Princeton Review®, one of the nation's leading education services companies, today reported findings of its third annual Campus Mental Health Services Survey. The 2026 survey is a part of a comprehensive initiative the company conducts in partnership with the Ruderman Family Foundation, an internationally recognized organization that works to end the stigma associated with mental health.

The project, which launched in October 2023, is an ongoing partnership. Designed to drive improvements in how colleges support student mental health and well-being, it builds on the Foundation's extensive work with colleges and universities across the U.S. to identify gaps in mental health resources and encourage initiatives to make student well-being a greater priority.

"Over the last decade, our Foundation has worked with colleges and universities to better understand where students are being supported and where important gaps remain," said Jay Ruderman, President of the Ruderman Family Foundation. "We partnered with The Princeton Review to build something that didn't exist before: a way to make student well-being visible and comparable across higher education, so it becomes a priority for institutions and for the families choosing them. Three years into the effort, we are encouraged by the progress we are seeing, but the ultimate measure of success will be whether institutions use what we are learning to make meaningful, lasting changes for their students."

The 2026 findings reported today are in two parts. The first reports on The Princeton Review's survey of administrators at 739 undergraduate institutions about their school's mental health and wellness services. The second reports on its survey of more than 56,000 students across 300 colleges about their awareness of those services. The full 2026 Campus Mental Health Services Survey Report is available for download and includes an executive summary, details on each survey and its methodology, survey questions and answer choices, and data analyses with year-over-year comparisons.

The growth in participation among schools suggests that comprehensive, campus-wide approaches to student mental health are no longer the exception; rather, they are increasingly becoming the norm among participating institutions. The Princeton Review and the Ruderman Family Foundation plan to evolve the project's Mental Health Services Honor Roll in 2027 to reflect that progress.

Year-over-Year Comparisons

Comparisons of survey findings—from the 2024 inaugural survey to the 2026 survey—show significant growth in many areas. Since the project's inception, institutional participation in the survey has nearly tripled from 250 participating institutions in 2024 to 540 in 2025 to 739 in 2026. Student participation has increased 409% from more than 11,000 students participating in the 2024 survey to more than 56,000 students participating in the 2026 survey. Finally, mental health education has become embedded in the academic curriculum. More than three quarters (77%) of institutions participating in the 2026 survey now offer for-credit or non-credit mental health and wellness education courses—compared with 58% so reporting in 2024.

Additional Findings of the 2026 Administrator Survey

Among the administrators at 739 institutions that completed the survey:

  • 99% (730) reported their colleges have a comprehensive mental health/wellness program that makes counseling, referral, and well-being services available to all students—up 41% from 515 so reporting in 2025, and up 238% from 216 so reporting in 2024
  • 99% (732) reported their colleges have a mental health services website—up 41% from 516 so reporting in 2025, and up 238% from 216 so reporting in 2024
  • 92% (371) reported their colleges have suicide prevention training programs—up 32% from 282 so reporting in 2025, and up 111% from 176 so reporting in 2024

Additional Findings of the 2026 Student Survey

Among the more than 56,000 students across 300 colleges that completed the survey:  

  • 82% agreed with the statement "If I needed to seek professional help for my mental or emotional health, I would know where to access my school's resources"—up from 79% so reporting on the 2025 survey
  • 80% agreed with the statement "Mental health services are readily available on campus"—up from 76% so reporting on the 2025 survey
  • 79% agreed with the statement "I am aware of mental health outreach efforts by my school"—up from 75% so reporting on the 2025 survey

Now in their second year, individualized benchmark reports give participating schools a comparison of their campus mental health services and programs with those of similar institutions and with the broader group of participating schools. The reports provide each school with a clear picture of where it stands and help translate the project's findings into meaningful, sustained action on campuses nationwide.

"We are deeply grateful to the Ruderman Family Foundation for its ongoing support for this project and its compelling advocacy for mental health and wellness services," said Rob Franek, Editor-in-Chief of The Princeton Review. "For more than 40 years, our company has helped millions of students find and get into their best-fit colleges. However—as many students, parents, and educators know—getting in is only the beginning. The road from orientation to graduation brings challenges across many fronts for which support is often essential, if not crucial. When it comes to student success in college, well-being is everything."

School Profiles & Honors

The project includes two initiatives to promote information about specific schools' campus mental health services and make that information accessible to college students, college applicants, parents, and student advisors.

  • The Princeton Review publishes information reported by administrators about their institution's campus mental health services in the company's profiles of the schools on its website and in its annual Best Colleges guide (now out in its 35th edition).   • Graduates saw an even larger average salary increase (33 percent) three years after degree completion.

  • An overwhelming majority of graduates (85 percent) agree their degree was worth the investment.



  • 78 percent of graduates would recommend their degree program to a friend or colleague.



  • The ability to continue working was the top reason for choosing online over on-campus or hybrid (59 percent), and 99 percent stayed employed during their program.



  • 89 percent agree that, because of their online degree, they were able to continue living and working in their local communities.

releases.title: Chartwells Higher Education's New Campus Voices Report Finds Students Want Dining They Can Trust
releases.body:
• New Campus Voices report explores the experiences, emotions and everyday realities behind student dining decisions
  • Findings are based on conversations with more than 2,000 students across 300 focus groups and 50 campuses
  • Students point to consistency, flexibility, functional wellness and authentic human connection as key parts of the dining experience

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Students are looking for more than endless choice from campus dining. They want food and experiences they can count on, options that fit the realities of their schedules and needs, and meaningful human connection along the way.

That is the central finding of Campus Voices, a new report released today by Chartwells Higher Education based on conversations with more than 2,000 students across 300 focus groups and 50 campuses, which explores the experiences, emotions and everyday realities behind student dining decisions, including what builds trust, what creates value and what brings students back.

"Campus Voices helps us understand the 'why' behind the data by listening directly to students," said Janelle Craft, VP of Insights and Innovation at Chartwells Higher Education. "Across these conversations, our students consistently described dining as something that needs to fit real life. They want reliable, quality meal options that reflect their needs and schedules, and experiences that feel responsive and human."

Direct, in-person feedback from students across diverse regions, campus sizes and dining models revealed five core themes driving student decision-making today:

  • Choice without confidence isn't really a choice. Having numerous options matters less to students if consistency and reliability are lacking. Trust in the quality and expectation of meals determines whether they are willing to champion dining options.
  • Variety is personal. Students report that variety, for them, is defined by the number of options that realistically fit their individual dietary needs, schedules and budgets. Customization serves as both a primary trust mechanism and a source of variety.
  • Value is an experience, not a price. Students evaluate meal value based on quality, completeness, convenience, flexibility and reliability. Perceived value is heavily influenced by balanced sides, fresh fruit and vegetables and thoughtful meal bundles.
  • Traditional mealtime is disappearing. Students no longer structure their days around traditional breakfast, lunch and dinner hours. Snacking and mobile pickups are increasing in popularity to meet students where they are.
  • The more digital dining becomes, the more human connection matters. Students report that while technology reduces operational friction, personal connections with dining staff and peers foster a sense of belonging on campus and make wait times feel shorter.

"Students want dining that fits their lives, but they also want to feel connected to the people and community around them," said Eva Wojtalewski, CEO of Chartwells Higher Education. "The food matters, but so does the welcome, the familiar face, and knowing that someone is paying attention. Their feedback is helping us create dining experiences that respond to the needs of each campus and help students feel seen."

Feedback from students shows that global flavors are now standard, and cuisine is judged based on how authentically it is prepared and how culturally appropriate the recipes are. Students also show strong demand for meals that are high in protein, minimally processed, and nutrient-rich so they feel energized and ready for their day. Campus dining events, including pop-ups, cultural celebrations and chef events, came up again and again as things students crave, and they make dining interactive, fostering valuable connections.

The findings will directly inform how Chartwells continues to evolve its menus, services and dining experiences across campuses, turning feedback into action. 

Campus Voices joins the 2026 Campus Dining Index and the Campus Dining Signal Report as part of Chartwells Higher Education's ongoing work to understand student perspectives and where expectations are headed.

Click here to download the full 2026 Campus Voices Report.

About Chartwells Higher Education  

Chartwells Higher Education, a part of Compass Group North America, is the recognized leader in contract foodservice management, hospitality, and guest service at more than 320 colleges and universities across the United States. Chartwells delivers "Dining, Made Personal" through quality, craveable food and dining programs tailored to each campus and designed around real student life. With signature service and meaningful connections, Chartwells partners with institutions to co-create campus experiences that make students and guests feel seen and welcomed.

Scholarships, transfer credits and prior-learning pathways help eligible students identify cost savings and affordability of degree completion

PHOENIX, Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix is recognizing National Transfer Student Week by highlighting the range of pathways that can help eligible students reduce education costs and make informed decisions about their educational journeys. Scholarships, transfer credits, prior learning assessments and alternative credit pathways offer students opportunities to gain insights about affordability and saving time and money on earning a degree while building on previous academic and professional achievements. 

"Many students assume affordability depends on a single scholarship or financial aid source," said Director of Financial Education Initiatives and Repayment Management, Chris Conway. "In reality, transfer credit, scholarship opportunities, prior learning and alternative credit pathways can work together to help reduce costs and create a more efficient path to degree completion. Understanding those options early can make a meaningful difference for students."

As University of Phoenix celebrates its 50th anniversary in 2026, the institution is reflecting five decades of helping working adults build on previous academic achievement and professional experience rather than start over. Today, transfer-credit pathways and scholarship opportunities remain an important part of that mission, helping eligible students reduce costs while pursuing degrees aligned with career goals.

Impact of Transfer-friendly programs

Affordable education pathways can help students continue pursuing their goals through life's most challenging seasons. For University of Phoenix transfer student Melonie Olipant, transfer credits helped her return to school after having children and continue making progress toward degree completion.

"Everyone expects a mother to say, 'I'm doing it for my children,' and they have always been a huge part of my why," Olipant said. "But there were moments when I was so tired, overwhelmed and lost that I didn't even know who I was doing it for anymore. I was so busy trying to hold everything together that I lost sight of myself.

"Still, I kept going not because I always felt strong, but because I refused to let the hardest season of my life become the ending of my story. Now, only a few credits away from my degree, I realize I wasn't just fighting for a better future for my children. I was fighting for myself, too. I didn't just earn a degree. I gave myself a future I once wasn't sure I'd see."

Scholarships help students reduce education costs

University of Phoenix offers multiple scholarship opportunities for eligible students like Olipant, ensuring that every new, qualifying student receives financial assistance. The Phoenix® Scholarship is available to students with at least three years of work experience, while the Transfer Scholarship is for those with 12 to 60 transfer credits.

  • Phoenix® Scholarship Savings Breakdown:

Bachelor's, Master's and Doctoral: Maximum value of $1K, provided the student maintains eligibility, applied over a set number of courses.

  • Transfer Scholarship Savings Breakdown:

In addition to University scholarships, alternate credit providers like Straighterline, Sophia and Study.com offer students an opportunity to earn general education credits via self-paced courses. Eligible students may complete general education courses with an alternative credit provider and then transfer eligible credits to University of Phoenix, helping them save time and money.

In addition to scholarships, transfer credit opportunities and alternate credit providers, University of Phoenix offers a comprehensive Savings Explorer® tool that presents information about scholarship opportunities, as well as transferring college credit and earning credit for prior learning through Prior Learning Assessment, national testing programs, alternative credit providers, and military service. By answering a few simple questions via the Savings Explorer tool, prospective students can find out what other students with relevant experience have saved.

University of Phoenix students and alumni have access to the Career Services for Life® commitment, helping to ensure the tools, resources, and support needed to thrive in their career of choice.

University of Phoenix is Built for Real Life. 50 Years Strong. The University innovates to help working adults enhance their careers and develop skills in a rapidly changing world through flexible online learning, relevant courses, academic AI pillars, and skills-mapped curriculum for associate, bachelor's and master's degree programs. Active students and alumni have access to Career Services for Life® resources including career guidance and tools. For more information, visit phoenix.edu.

releases.title: WayUp Launches New Mobile App, Giving Students and Recent Grads a Faster Way to Catch Entry-Level Roles Before They Fill Up
releases.body:
CHICAGO, Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- WayUp, the job search and recruiting marketplace built exclusively for college students and early-career job seekers, today announced the launch of its redesigned mobile app for iOS and Android. The app sends real-time alerts the moment a followed company posts a new internship or entry-level role, and lets candidates apply using the resume, education, and experience already saved to their WayUp profile, removing the need to rebuild an application from scratch for every role.

The launch comes as the market for early-career hires has tightened measurably: recent-college-graduate unemployment reached roughly 5.6% in the second quarter of 2026, among the highest readings in a decade outside the pandemic, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. With fewer no-experience entry-level openings available and employers moving quickly once applications start arriving, how fast a candidate sees and acts on a posting has become a meaningful factor in getting noticed.

"Right now, nearly half of entry-level jobs that used to require zero experience have disappeared, and recent grad unemployment just hit its highest point in a decade outside the pandemic," said Amy Farr-Jones, VP Growth at WayUp. "Students aren't losing out because they're not qualified—they're losing out because they see the role three days too late. We built the new WayUp app so the moment a great entry-level role opens, the right person sees it first and can move on it immediately."

The app is free to download and use, available now on the App Store and Google Play. Existing WayUp users can log in with their current account and keep their saved profile; new users can sign up directly in the app.

For more information, visit wayup.com.

releases.body:
HelloCollege data shows widespread AI use in coursework, rising career anxiety and shifting views on majors and degrees

OAK BROOK, Ill., Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HelloCollege today released findings from its 2026 College Student AI Survey, showing that AI is already shaping how college students learn, plan and think about their futures. The survey found that 66% of current college students are more concerned about their future career because of AI, 50% say AI has changed how they understand the use of a college degree and 82% use AI in their coursework.

The findings suggest students are not just experimenting with AI. They are incorporating it into everyday academic life while also weighing what it could mean for the long-term value of higher education. As AI becomes more common in the classroom, students are asking bigger questions about whether a degree will still deliver the career security and return on investment they expected.

That uncertainty is already influencing decision-making. More than 1 in 3 (37%) students say they are shifting their career plans around AI, showing AI is changing not only how students complete their work but also how they choose their path forward.

"AI is not some far-off thing for students," said Kevin Krebs, founder and CEO of HelloCollege. "It is already part of how they study, how they search for colleges and how they think about what comes after graduation. What this survey shows is that students see the value in AI, but they are also getting nervous about where they fit in. They are asking real questions about which majors still make sense, which careers feel safer and whether a college degree is going to give them the kind of return they expected in a job market that is changing fast."

Student sentiment in the survey reflects that uncertainty. Over half (58%) of college students believe AI is not a net good for society, with the biggest concerns being mass layoffs, difficulty telling truth from fiction, data privacy, learning loss and mass surveillance.

At the same time, students see potential upside, with 25% saying their biggest hope for AI is better work conditions through automation, followed by more free time and new fields of employment.

"Entry-level IT professionals today must be able to catch that kind of deception quickly, and recognize when an AI tool's recommendation is wrong. Our students will develop the knowledge, skills, and judgment it takes to navigate this new world."

AI runs through the curriculum: students learn to spot AI-generated deception in early security scenarios, validate AI-assisted recommendations in network-defense labs, and study how AI is used on both sides of an attack.

"Students in this program will build and test network defenses, work step by step through simulated incidents, and have to justify every decision they make. That rigor is what prepares students for the day-to-day work of an entry-level security role" said Casey.

Students also leave prepared for the high-value, industry-recognized certifications employers often look for in entry-level hires. releases.title: College Student Mental Health: New AllOne Health Research Reveals Who Seeks Counseling and How They Access Care
releases.body:
Peer-reviewed research examines 2,800 counseling cases across 36 higher education institutions, revealing how students access support for mental health, relationship concerns, and everyday stress.

WILKES-BARRE, Pa., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Anxiety, depression, and grief were the leading reasons college students sought counseling through AllOne Health's Student Assistance Program (SAP), with mental health concerns accounting for 61% of cases, according to a pair of peer-reviewed studies published in the Journal of Education and Human Development. Students also reached out for help with personal relationships (19%) and everyday life stress (17%).

The research, announced today by AllOne Health, a leading provider of Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs), Student Assistance Programs (SAPs), and integrated whole health solutions, gives university presidents, student affairs professionals, healthcare service providers, and other campus leaders a data-driven view of what brings students to counseling, how quickly they connect with care, and how a Student Assistance Program can complement campus services.

"Today's college students bring a wide range of life experiences, schedules, and needs. Student Assistance Programs give institutions an innovative way to meet them," said Keith Wasley, President & CEO of AllOne Health. "When a student reaches out, fast access to high-quality clinical care and in-the-moment support makes the biggest impact. Our SAP is designed to complement campus student services by giving students a trusted place to turn, 24/7, by phone, app, or video."

What Brings Students to Counseling

The counseling study analyzed 2,800 cases from 36 colleges and universities across the United States between 2020 and 2024, examining why students sought support, how counseling was delivered, and how they used services. Students who used counseling represented a broad range of ages and life stages. Key findings include:

  • Mental health was the leading concern. Mental health issues accounted for 61% of cases, including anxiety (23%), depression and mood disorders (11%), grief and loss (5%), and other emotional issues (22%).
  • Relationships and everyday stress were also common. Personal relationship concerns accounted for 19% of cases, and personal life stress accounted for 17%.
  • Counseling was delivered almost entirely by video or phone. Based on the 1,986 cases with recorded modality, online video accounted for 89% of cases, telephone counseling for 10%, and in-person counseling for 1%.
  • Nearly 1 in 4 cases were resolved in a single session. Students used an average of 3.5 sessions over 47 days, and 24% of cases used just one session of counseling to resolve the student's concern.
  • The length of care varied with student needs. The largest share of cases used 2 or 3 sessions (42%), and about a third (34%) used 4 to 9 sessions, with sessions spaced about 18 days apart on average.
  • Students represented a broad range of ages. 27% of clients were of traditional undergraduate age (18 to 24), while 33% were 25 to 29 years old, 26% were in their 30s, and 14% were 40 to 75 years old.

Why It Matters for Higher Education

Among students who used the program, mental health concerns were the most common reason for seeking support, followed by relationship difficulties and everyday stress. With counseling available by video or phone, students can connect with care around their classes, work, and family responsibilities, when and where they need it.

"Through our partnerships with colleges and universities, AllOne Health's Student Assistance Program has been extending the reach of campus counseling centers, providing additional licensed clinical support aligned with each institution's student mental health initiatives, goals, and services," said Jason C. McDaniel, Regional Vice President of Operations at AllOne Health and co-author of the studies. "With nearly a quarter of cases in our study resolved in a single session, focused counseling helps our partner institutions support more students with the resources they already have."

Fast, Flexible Access When Students Reach Out

During intake, 11% of cases included a brief "In-the-Moment" telephone support call, and across the five-year study period, the first call was answered in about 16 seconds on average. Students most often began their requests for counseling by phone (70%) or through the mobile app (30%), both available 24/7.

"Students use counseling for many reasons, ranging from anxiety and depression to relationship difficulties and personal stress, and this mix differs slightly by age as well," said Mark Attridge, Ph.D., co-author of the study. "Understanding why and how students use counseling can help institutions consider the support resources needed by students in different age groups."

Practical Support for Daily Life

A companion study examined 5,604 work/life service cases among students at 29 colleges and universities. Personal life and convenience support accounted for 44% of those cases, followed by financial referrals (36%), legal referrals (12%), and childcare assistance (4%). Students used personal life concierge support at three times the rate of employees using AllOne Health's EAP work/life services over the same period (44% vs. 14%). Together, the two studies show how Student Assistance Programs can complement campus services by giving students access to both counseling and practical resources for real-life problems.

"The purpose of this research was to develop a clearer profile of students who use Student Assistance Program services, including the concerns that bring them to counseling and how they access support," said Dr. Attridge. "By documenting these service-use patterns and comparing them with existing research on campus counseling center users, we can better understand the role of external SAP services."

About the Research

The studies describe service utilization among AllOne Health program users. The samples were not designed to represent all college students in the United States, measure changes in student well-being or academic outcomes, or establish the effectiveness of a particular service model. The work-life study sample was especially concentrated among students attending large, private, for-profit institutions and fully online or hybrid schools.

Both studies were authored by Mark Attridge, Ph.D., M.A., of Attridge Consulting, Inc., and Jason C. McDaniel, LCSW, CEAP, MBA, of AllOne Health, and published in the Journal of Education and Human Development in March 2026. Dr. Attridge, an independent research consultant, was engaged by AllOne Health to conduct the studies. McDaniel is an AllOne Health executive.

GRAND RAPIDS, Mich., Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A GRCC Raider today. A WMU Bronco tomorrow. For Grand Rapids Community College students dreaming of earning a bachelor's degree, that next step is about to become a lot more certain.

Through a new partnership called the Bronco Bound Guarantee, students who earn an associate degree at GRCC will be guaranteed admission to Western Michigan University, along with an annual scholarship ranging from $1,000 to $4,500 for eligible students.

Leaders from both institutions will make the partnership official during a signing ceremony at 3 p.m. Friday, Oct. 16, at GRCC's Applied Technology Center, Secchia Piazza, on the college's main campus in Grand Rapids. Media are invited to attend.

"Strong partnerships create strong pathways for students. This agreement reflects a shared commitment to making higher education more accessible, affordable and connected," said GRCC President Dr. Kathryn A. Rogalski. "We are proud to partner with Western Michigan University, an institution that recognizes the quality of a GRCC education and the strong foundation our students bring to their next chapter. Together, we are creating more opportunities for students to achieve their educational goals and build a brighter future for themselves and our communities."

The Bronco Bound Guarantee is designed to take some uncertainty out of transferring from community college to a four-year university.

"Having led a community college, I know the important role these institutions play in helping students discover their potential and pursue their goals," said WMU President Russ Kavalhuna.

"Our partnership with Grand Rapids Community College builds on that foundation. We want students to arrive at Western knowing they belong here, find opportunities to put their learning into practice and have the support to thrive, graduate, and build meaningful careers."

In addition to guaranteed admission, qualifying GRCC students will have their WMU application fee waived and receive scholarship consideration automatically, with eligible students guaranteed an annual award of $1,000 to $4,500.

Students will also have access to dedicated transfer advising and recommended academic plans to help them make the most of their credits. Those who can complete an associate degree through an approved transfer guide or program agreement will have their defined credits apply toward the corresponding WMU degree requirements, avoiding the frustration of losing credits along the way.

And students won't have to wait until their first day at WMU to begin feeling like Broncos.

Prior to admission, eligible students will enjoy early access to university resources and campus experiences, including free admission to WMU sporting events, excluding hockey.

The partnership is about more than providing a route to admission. It is also about helping students make a successful transition into university life, connect with the Bronco community and take advantage of distinctive academic programs and experiential learning opportunities.

The partnership also recognizes the importance of completing a GRCC credential. Through a no-cost reverse transfer process, students who continue their education at WMU can have eligible university credits transferred back to GRCC to help them earn an associate degree.

GRCC and WMU will continue working together beyond the signing ceremony, with WMU participating in at least one transfer-focused event each semester and both institutions reviewing student enrollment and achievement data to strengthen the partnership.

For GRCC students, Bronco Bound means the journey toward a bachelor's degree can begin with greater confidence, knowing their next opportunity is already within reach.

GRCC was established in 1914 — Michigan's first community college — and is focused on making college education accessible and affordable. Classes are scheduled weekdays, evenings and Saturdays in Grand Rapids, Holland and online. We offer traditional liberal arts and occupational career pathways, adult education courses and skilled training courses and apprenticeships.

WMU students are individuals who are truly unique. At Western, we celebrate the passions that drive students and the possibilities that inspire them. For us, a degree is a pursuit of purpose where students are empowered to learn and where an experience-driven education leads to a meaningful career. Broncos prosper. Nine out of 10 graduates are employed quickly, working in their field in jobs they like. WMU students make their mark on the world—Grammy recipients, Super Bowl champions, doctors, teachers, pilots and countless others have flourished here. releases.body:
SAN ANTONIO, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As Texas A&M University-San Antonio's enrollment reached 7,697 students in Fall 2026, including a record 1,322 first-time-in-college students, the University is working to ensure that the cost of higher education does not stand in the way of opportunity.

That commitment is reflected in Jaguar Promise, a scholarship program designed to make college more affordable for eligible Texas residents, including transfer students and adult learners. With 60% of A&M-San Antonio students eligible for federal Pell Grants, the program plays an important role in helping students pursue their degrees with less financial burden.

As a last-dollar scholarship, Jaguar Promise, which launched in 2024, covers remaining tuition and mandatory fees after eligible federal, state and institutional financial aid is applied. Participants also receive a $300-per-semester book stipend.

Participation continues to grow. The number of first-year students receiving Jaguar Promise funding increased 21% over the previous year. Among first-year participants, enrollment grew 48% among Early College High School graduates and 9% among students who graduated in the top 10% to 35% of their high school class.

"Jaguar Promise has made a meaningful difference in my college experience," said Student Body President Caroleena Mancilla. "Knowing that my tuition and fees are covered has allowed me to focus more on my education, leadership opportunities and personal growth instead of constantly worrying about how I will pay for college. That support has opened the door to experiences that are helping me grow both personally and professionally."

Beyond helping students afford college, Jaguar Promise supports the University's broader efforts to promote student persistence and degree completion. Program requirements include maintaining a minimum 12-credit-hour course load each semester and meeting established GPA and academic progress standards.

The University is also working with Alamo Colleges District through its Promise-to-Promise partnership, which helps eligible students transition from an associate degree to a bachelor's degree while pursuing a more affordable, debt-free path to graduation.

"Affordability can make the difference between whether students simply aspire to attend college and whether they can turn that aspiration into a degree," said Brandy McLelland, vice president for enrollment management. "The growing participation in Jaguar Promise reflects the importance of providing students and families with a clear, affordable path to higher education. By reducing financial barriers and supporting students as they progress toward graduation, we are advancing our commitment to access and student success."

That commitment extends to the University's expanding academic offerings, which are designed to connect students with emerging career opportunities across San Antonio and South Texas. In Fall 2026, A&M-San Antonio launched its first doctoral program, the Doctor of Education in Educational Leadership. The University will also introduce a Bachelor of Science in Biomedical Sciences in Fall 2027, with programs in electrical engineering, healthcare administration and management, computer engineering, and construction engineering technology planned for subsequent years.

For President Salvador Hector Ochoa, the University's growth reflects a broader commitment to expanding opportunity while responding to the needs of the region.

"As A&M-San Antonio grows, our responsibility remains the same: to open doors to higher education and help more students achieve their goals," Ochoa said. "We are expanding academic opportunities and strengthening our research enterprise while keeping affordability and student success at the center of our mission. Our true measure of success is when we create lasting opportunities for the students, families and communities we serve."

Flash Mentoring joins Mentor Collective's existing Structured Mentoring model to support the full arc of the student journey, from belonging to employability, on one platform.

Higher education institutions are under unprecedented pressure to demonstrate career readiness, workforce outcomes, and degree ROI. Many students, including first-generation, low-income, and underrepresented students, still lack access to the professional networks that open doors, and not every student is looking for, or has time for, a long-term match. Mentor Collective meets students right where they are. With Flash Mentoring, every student has a low-barrier way to build real-world social capital on their own terms: whenever they need it, and as often as they need it, with no long-term commitment required.

"Every student's path looks different, and their support should too," said Patrick Garayta, Chief Executive Officer of Mentor Collective. "Some students want an ongoing relationship with a peer mentor. Others need the right person with the right experience for one purposeful conversation. Flash Mentoring and Structured Mentoring are built for exactly that reason, and together, they mean no students' needs will fall through the cracks."

Flash Mentoring is also designed with alumni in mind. Traditional engagement strategies, from reunions to newsletters to committee service, reach only a small fraction of a given alumni base. Flash offers a flexible, time-boxed way for alumni to give back in a single conversation, activating graduates who would never respond to a longer commitment. At the same time, advancement and alumni relations teams gain a new, trackable form of engagement to bring to leadership.

"Career offices and advancement teams keep telling us the same thing: their networks are bigger than their engagement numbers show," said Jennifer Kious, Director of Marketing at Mentor Collective. "Flash Mentoring is specifically built to reach the alumni who are typically disengaged. Every conversation becomes data our partners can use to tell a clearer story about alumni engagement and student outcomes."

Flash Mentoring gives every student a low-barrier way to build that access: a focused conversation with an alum around a specific question or goal, without the long-term commitment of a traditional mentoring program. For alumni, it offers a meaningful, flexible way to give back on their own schedule. For institutions, every conversation becomes a logged, reportable data point that strengthens the case for continued investment in student success.

Many students, including first-generation, low-income, and underrepresented students, still lack access to the professional networks that open doors, and not every student is looking for, or has time for, a long-term match. ALBUQUERQUE, N.M., Oct. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Prominently featured in The Inner Circle, Dr. Joseph G. R. Martinez is acknowledged as a Pinnacle Professional of The Year for his contributions to Mathematics Education and Student Success.

Dr. Joseph G. R. Martinez has built a distinguished career in higher education, dedicating nearly four decades to teaching and advancing mathematics education. As a retired faculty member of the University of New Mexico, he is recognized for his commitment to student success and his ability to make complex mathematical concepts accessible to learners at all levels.

Dr. Martinez specialized in mathematics education, graduate statistics, calculus, and algebra, with a particular focus on reducing math anxiety. His teaching approach emphasized patience and step by step instruction, helping students build confidence and develop a deeper understanding of mathematical principles. His methods have inspired many students to pursue further studies and careers in mathematics.

He earned a Doctor of Philosophy in Education and Mathematics, with concentrations in mathematics education and educational psychology, from the University of New Mexico in 1980. His academic background provided a strong foundation for his work in both teaching and research design.

Throughout his career, Dr. Martinez taught at the University of New Mexico until his retirement in 2012 and also held earlier teaching roles at the University of Albuquerque. Over the years, he became widely respected for his engaging teaching style and dedication to supporting student achievement.

In addition to his work in the classroom, Dr. Martinez is an accomplished author, having written eight books and more than 200 published articles. His book Math Without Fear, along with other works including those coauthored with his late wife Nancy, reflects his mission to make mathematics more approachable and less intimidating for students.

Dr. Martinez credits his wife, Nancy, as a key influence in refining his teaching philosophy and instructional methods. Her support and insight played an important role in shaping his approach to education.

Looking ahead, Dr. Martinez is exploring opportunities to expand his educational outreach, particularly within Orthodox Jewish communities. Guided by a philosophy that anyone can learn mathematics with the right support and instruction, he remains committed to sharing his knowledge and helping others overcome challenges in learning.

Students who participate in the University Partnerships program are more likely to persist through college than their peers: 85% of freshmen continue on to their sophomore year, and 57-100% graduate from college within five years, 3-5 times the national average, reducing the likelihood of accruing unnecessary educational debt and opening the door to greater economic and career opportunities.

As a DC CAP University Partner, American University certifies its commitment to ensuring every college-ready D.C. student has the financial resources, coaching, and community they need to succeed. American University will collaborate closely with DC CAP to maximize financial aid availability, stacking DC CAP scholarships, Pell Grants, D.C. Tuition Assistance Grants (DCTAG), and institutional aid with the goal of helping D.C. students finish college with little to no debt. "For so many of our scholars, staying close to the community they grew up in matters, and having one of the nation's top universities just a short Metro ride away means they don't have to choose between a great education and home," said Eric Waldo, executive director of DC CAP. "We couldn't be more thrilled to be joining forces with American University. This partnership will help turn proximity into opportunity, and ensure that more students in the District can access the support they need to learn and thrive."

Students who are interested in participating in DC CAP programs can confirm their eligibility by taking a short online survey, which opens on October 15, and then applying in January 2027. For more information, please visit www.dccap.org/programs/university-partners.

The social mobility ranking measures how successfully universities enroll and graduate students from economically disadvantaged backgrounds. Approximately 60% of A&M-San Antonio students are Pell Grant-eligible, reflecting the University's mission to expand access to higher education and create pathways to opportunity. NEW YORK, Sept. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Princeton Review®, a provider of education services and college admission resources since 1981, today released the 35th edition of its annual guide to getting funding to pay for college.

Paying for College: Everything You Need to Maximize Financial Aid and Afford College (2027 Edition, Penguin Random House, September 22, 2026, $25.99) is authored by Kalman A. Chany, a nationally recognized expert on college funding, with Geoff Martz. Chany is founder and president of Campus Consultants Inc., an independent college financial aid advisory firm based in New York City.

When Paying for College debuted in 1992, it was a one-of-a-kind resource in the category of personal finance guides. It provided detailed line-by-line guidance on strategically completing the two most important financial aid application forms for the upcoming aid application year, and it was the only book to do so.

Paying for College remains the only resource offering such targeted guidance for submitting those two crucial forms. They are the U.S. Department of Education's FAFSA® (Free Application for Federal Student Aid), which all financial aid applicants must submit, and the College Board's CSS Profile®, an application that hundreds of selective colleges require (and which has as many as 200 questions).

"You might think that families who receive the most financial aid would be the families with the most need," Chany says in the introduction of the book. "In fact, this is not necessarily true. The people who receive the most aid are the people who best understand the aid process." 

Chany well understands the process. Since 1981, he has annually analyzed the major aid application forms as well as the formulas by which federal and institutional financial aid administrators assess an applicant's need for aid based on answers on the forms. He guides his clients (and readers of this book) on how to maximize their eligibility for financial aid much in the same way an accountant advises clients on submitting their IRS returns to their best advantage. (All the strategies Chany recommends follow the law to the letter.)

In Paying for College, Chany also covers other subjects important to aid applicants and parents, including how to:

  • explore long- and short-term strategies for reducing college costs
  • research colleges with financial aid in mind
  • compare financial aid offers and, if necessary, appeal for more aid
  • obtain education loans, understand payment plans, and manage loan debt

A Special Topics chapter in the book gives particular advice on aid applications for parents who are single, separated, divorced or in blended families as well as advice for students who are independent, international or older than the traditional applicant.

The 2027 edition of Paying for College also reports on tectonic changes that have impacted the college funding landscape as a result of various provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) signed into law in July 2025. Chany discusses what parents and students need to know about these changes. Icons in the margins flag topics that were pending as the book went to press that readers are advised to check.

Some provisions of the OBBBA that impact federal student aid are still unresolved. "Unfortunately," Chany notes, "some guidance involving federal education loans issued by the U.S. Department of Education is being misinterpreted—even by college aid professionals."

Over the years, Paying for College has been praised by reviewers and finance professionals alike. Forbes contributor John Wasik noted it "can save thousands in college bills." Washington Post syndicated columnist Michelle Singletary chose it for her Color of Money book club. Newsday Family Finance columnist Lynn Brenner recommended it as "a first-rate guide through the financial aid maze."

Said Rob Franek, Editor-in-Chief of The Princeton Review, "Our company has a deep appreciation for the concerns of students and parents about paying for college. Among nearly 10,000 college applicants and parents of applicants who completed our 2026 College Hopes & Worries Survey in February, 93% reported they would need financial aid to pay for college, and 81% of that cohort characterized their level of need as "very" or "extremely" necessary. We hope the advice in this new edition of Paying for College will help parents and students apply strategies to get all the financial aid they are entitled to and enable them to pay less for college."

Paying for College is one of more than 150 books developed by The Princeton Review and published by Penguin Random House in a line that includes The Best 392 Colleges  and guides to the SAT®, ACT®, and AP® exams. The Princeton Review is also known for its annual college rankings in dozens of categories including its popular "Great Financial Aid" college ranking list and its "Best Value Colleges" lists.

Kalman A. Chany is the founder and president of Campus Consultants Inc., an independent New York City-based financial aid advisory firm. For more than four decades, his firm has helped thousands of families maximize their financial aid eligibility and save tens of thousands of dollars off the cost of their children's college education. Kal has been sourced in The Wall Street Journal, on CNBC, and in Money magazine, and he has appeared on CBS Evening News, NBC Nightly News, and other broadcast media.

About The Princeton Review

The Princeton Review is a leading tutoring, test prep, and college admissions services company. Every year, it helps millions of college- and graduate school–bound students as well as working professionals achieve their education and career goals through its many education services and products. These include online and in-person courses delivered by a network of more than 4,000 teachers and tutors; online resources; a line of more than 150 print and digital books published by Penguin Random House; and dozens of categories of school rankings. Founded in 1981, the company is now in its 45th year. The company's Tutor.com brand, now in its 25th year, is one of the largest online tutoring services in the U.S. It comprises a community of thousands of tutors who have delivered more than 29 million tutoring sessions. releases.body:
BUFFALO, N.Y., Sept. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- BetterMynd, a leading online therapy platform centered on the mental health needs of university and college students, has announced a partnership with Lavender Psychiatry, the largest nurse-led online psychiatry and therapy practice in the United States. Together, the organizations will expand access to flexible, high-quality care by integrating Lavender's medication management services into the BetterMynd therapeutic ecosystem.

With one in three students reporting symptoms of moderate anxiety or depression (Healthy Minds, 2025), the demand for accessible care is at an all-time high. This partnership reflects a shared belief that students are best served by adaptable care models built around the individual. By combining their expertise, BetterMynd and Lavender can better respond to the full spectrum of mental health needs seen across the student population.

For educational institutions navigating growing demand and increasing complexity in student mental health, the partnership offers a high-quality, scalable solution that is easy to implement.

"Our mission is to make getting help easier for every college student, and we believe every student deserves an exceptional experience," said Cody Semrau, Founder and CEO of BetterMynd. "We're excited to partner with Lavender, an organization that shares our mission-driven focus and also puts the students first in all that they do. This ensures students have the most comprehensive resources available while providing institutions with a trusted, scalable model."

Accessing psychiatric care can often mean navigating long wait times, referrals between multiple providers, and limited prescribing options; barriers that can be especially challenging for student populations. Lavender removes this friction by providing integrated psychiatric services within BetterMynd's established care pathway, from assessment and prescribing to ongoing medication management, including ADHD treatment and controlled substances when clinically appropriate. With virtual appointments typically available within one week, students can get the support they need without lengthy delays. A network of 150+ board-certified psychiatric nurse practitioners across more than 40 states, supported by customized referral pathways and dedicated administrative support, helps make that access seamless and scalable for BetterMynd's university partners.

"We believe in creating a world where feelings are respected and cared for. BetterMynd shares our passion for making kind, effective, high-quality care more accessible," said Pritma Dhillon-Chattha, DNP, MHA, RN, Co-Founder of Lavender. "Mental health journeys are unique and we're reflecting that in our joint adaptable approach to therapy and medication management. By embedding Lavender's online psychiatry services naturally into the BetterMynd community, we're making the student journey more seamless and serving as a true extension of the campus counseling center."

The partnership is currently live at select institutions. Both organizations will continue to build and expand access across multiple states and campuses throughout 2026 and beyond.

About BetterMynd

BetterMynd is a leading online therapy platform designed specifically to meet the mental health needs of college students. BetterMynd supplements and expands on-campus resources by providing personalized care and scheduling flexibility. Serving more than 100 colleges and universities, BetterMynd reaches over 500,000 students through a network of 400+ licensed clinicians. Learn more at www.bettermynd.com.

About Lavender

Lavender Psychiatry is the largest nurse-owned and operated online psychiatry and therapy office in the U.S. Founded on the principle that care should be kind, collaborative and effective, Lavender provides timely access to high-quality therapy and medication management through 150+ board-certified psychiatric nurse practitioners across 40+ states. The practice also works with partners by integrating select services into existing mental health care ecosystems. Learn more at www.joinlavender.com.

At a Glance

  • This fall, the U.S. Army National Guard's mixed-reality experience, Disasterville, is returning to high schools nationwide to show students how National Guard Soldiers respond to natural disasters and emergencies. 
  • Disasterville guides students through high-tech, virtual missions to tackle wildfires, floods, and earthquakes in the same way as the Guard.
