WASHINGTON, Sept. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- This fall, the Army National Guard's immersive mixed-reality experience, Disasterville, will begin its second nationwide tour of high schools, giving students a first-hand look at how to prepare for and respond to natural disasters—without leaving their schools. Disasterville is activating in high school gyms where it will take students through virtual missions to tackle wildfires, floods, and earthquakes, just like Soldiers responding to similar emergencies in communities across the country. This follows Disasterville's successful inaugural tour in spring 2026, which reached more than 2,000 students.

"Natural disasters are not slowing down, and Army National Guard Soldiers are playing a critical role in response efforts across the country," says Lt. Col. Sabrina Zowada, Chief of the National Guard Bureau's Marketing and Advertising Branch. "Disasterville is a one-of-a-kind perspective for students to see how and when the Guard is showing up in their communities, and experience the real skills and impact of these important missions." 

Disasterville is transforming high school gyms from September through November in the following cities: Memphis, Tenn.; Chicago, Ill.; Hagerstown, Md.; Philadelphia, Pa.; Long Island, N.Y.; Richmond, Va.; and Atlanta, Ga.

Students Work Together to Respond to Common Missions

Disasterville uses advanced mixed-reality technology to create three 10-minute missions most common to Army National Guard response efforts. Working together in teams of five, students are called to service at the following sites:

  • Wildfire: Amid a raging wildfire, teams work together to push back fires encroaching on a home in Disaster Canyon. Students will put out small wildfires, combine forces to push back larger flare-ups, save animals, and dodge falling trees. 
  • Flood Zone: After a major hurricane, civilians are fighting to stay above water on the streets they call home. Students will board their Zodiac and use headlamps to find and safely evacuate survivors while avoiding dangerous wildlife and other lurking hazards.
  • Earthquake: After a devastating earthquake, a train carrying hazardous chemicals and passengers derails, pinning civilians and spilling dangerous material, poisoning the air. Time ticks down as students arm themselves with the jaws of life to rescue survivors and clean up debris, all before the train gives way under its own weight.

"We saw firsthand how students connected with the Disasterville experience. They didn't just learn about disaster response—they felt the responsibility," says Lt. Col. Zawada. "Today's young people want purpose; they want action, and they want to know how they can contribute to something meaningful. We're excited to show even more students how the Guard meets that need."

Mixed-Reality Technology Brings Immersion and Impact

Disasterville utilizes advanced mixed-reality technology with augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) graphics mapped to large plywood structures, creating a free-roam virtual neighborhood experience in high school gyms. Students wear virtual reality headsets with multiplayer, local-network tracking to engage with classmates in-game as the structures around them become devastated buildings, debris, rough terrain, and hazards, rescuing people in need. The technology also features advanced hand tracking, eliminating the need for game controllers and allowing students to interact with others and physically use in-game props and Army National Guard rescue tools like oars, hoses, chainsaws, and the jaws of life.  

Extended reality (XR) industry expert Dale Carman helped the Army bring the Disasterville experience to life. Carman is the co-founder and executive creative director at Groove Jones, which has over 25 years of experience in feature films, immersive tech, and branded productions.

A specialized tour crew will be present at each tour stop to guide participants safely through each mission. Army National Guard recruiters will also be available to connect with students and answer questions about service.   

For more information on the Army National Guard, visit NationalGuard.com.

Supplementary Information

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is Disasterville, and how does the experience work?

A: Disasterville is a mixed-reality experience from the U.S. Army National Guard touring the nation, transforming gymnasiums into full-scale, mission-oriented disaster zones to show students how National Guard Soldiers respond to natural disasters and emergencies through hands-on simulations. Students wear Meta Quest 3 headsets with multiplayer, local-network tracking to engage with classmates in-game as the structures around them become devastated buildings, debris, rough terrain, hazards, and people in need. Students are guided firsthand through high-tech, virtual missions, working together in teams to tackle three disaster zones -- wildfire, flood zone, and earthquake -- the same way as the Guard, by combining communication, physical endurance, and ingenuity to save lives, landscape, and their communities.

Q: Where will Disasterville be traveling?

A: Following a successful 2026 spring tour, Disasterville will head to even more high schools September through November in the following cities: Memphis, Tenn.; Chicago, Ill.; Hagerstown, Md.; Philadelphia, Pa.; Long Island, N.Y.; Richmond, Va.; and Atlanta, Ga. At each tour stop, a specialized tour crew will ensure the safety of and guide participants through each mission. Army National Guard recruiters will also be available to connect with students and answer questions about Guard service.   

Q: What do Army National Guard Soldiers do? Where and how do they serve?

A: With a presence in 54 states and territories, the Army National Guard is a unique component of the U.S. Army where Soldiers serve part-time to support communities in their home state by responding to domestic emergencies and at the federal level as standby support for Active Duty Soldiers. Serving at least one weekend a month and two weeks a year, National Guard Soldiers have the flexibility to pursue their civilian personal and professional passions.

Q: Where can I learn more about opportunities in the Army National Guard?

A: For more information on the opportunities in the National Guard, visit NationalGuard.com.

About the Army National Guard (ARNG):

With a presence in 54 states and territories, the Army National Guard is a unique component of the U.S. Army where Soldiers support communities in their home state by responding to domestic emergencies and at the federal level as standby support for Active Duty Soldiers. Army National Guard Soldiers have the flexibility to serve part-time across medical, aviation, law enforcement, transportation, and engineering fields and beyond, while also pursuing their personal and professional goals through a civilian career or higher education. For more information on the opportunities in the National Guard, visit NationalGuard.com.

releases.body:
Researchers see a 10-percentage-point increase in retention rates for Arizona State University students participating in Podium's work-integrated program.

AUSTIN, Texas, Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Podium Education released findings from independent research showing that undergraduate college students who participate in its flagship experience, the Global Career Accelerator (The Accelerator), have significantly higher college retention rates than peers who did not participate.

The Accelerator is a for-credit academic initiative that offers students work-integrated learning within their college curriculum. The Accelerator aims to boost career readiness for students by rotating participants through immersive projects and live experiences co-designed with Podium's 50-plus industry partners, including Crocs, L'Oreal, and Wells Fargo.

Through an innovative student success research partnership between Podium, the University of California, Irvine, and Arizona State University (ASU), UC Irvine researchers tracked over 350,000 ASU students across three academic cohorts from 2021-2022 through 2023-2024. The findings show that students who completed Podium's Accelerator remained enrolled in subsequent semesters at rates 6 to 10 percentage points higher than non-participants year over year.

In a matched-sample analysis, which paired nearly 3,000 participants with demographically and academically similar peers, participants were retained at 90%, compared to 86% for matched non-participants. Additionally, researchers found statistically significant improvements in retention after controlling for factors like first-generation status, Pell eligibility, online versus on-campus enrollment, race, and GPA.

"The consistency of this finding across three years and two distinct analytic methods points to the exciting results of this experiential programming," said Richard Arum, Professor of Sociology and Education at UC Irvine.

"The results of this study are promising," said Anne Jones, ASU vice provost for undergraduate education. "The ASU Global Career Accelerator helps students see how their academic experience connects to the world of work. That kind of relevance can be powerful in keeping students engaged and on track to complete their degree."

Podium's innovative platform is available to more than 1.7 million students, including over 550,000 who are Pell-eligible, across more than 100 university partners. The program is backed by leading industry partners ranging from large technology organizations like Intel to consumer brands like Procter & Gamble, to non-profits like charity: water.

Increasing demand for work-integrated college experiences is driving Podium's growth. Recent data from the Business-Higher Education Forum reports that the gap between internship interest among college students and availability is a growing concern. While 8.2M learners in the U.S. reported wanting one annually, only an estimated 2.5M high-quality internships are available.

The Accelerator was designed to close that gap by embedding real, credit-bearing work experience directly into the degree, with no prerequisites, so access doesn't depend on a student's major, financial means, or ability to relocate.

"This research is the first large-scale, independent confirmation of what we've seen anecdotally since day one — that when students get real, embedded work experience, they see a brighter future for themselves and stay in college," said Chris Parrish, Co-Founder and President at Podium Education. "We're committed to expanding our partnerships with institutions to offer more industry-integrated academic experiences to both drive stronger retention for schools and better return on investment for students."

About the Research

UC Irvine researchers Richard Arum and Jeffrey M. DeVries independently conducted and reported the study, in collaboration with Jennifer Malerich of Arizona State University, and the UC Irvine Institutional Review Board reviewed and approved it. The UC Irvine research team maintained full analytic independence throughout.

A full accounting of methodology, including cohort-specific and propensity-score-matched models, is available to download: HERE.

About Podium Education

Podium Education is the leading experiential education company partnering with universities and industry to embed scalable, real-world, high-impact practices directly into the undergraduate degree for credit. Podium works with more than 100 universities, including ASU, Penn State, and Rice, and 50+ leading industry partners like L'Oréal, OpenAI, and Wells Fargo. Podium's experiences deliver fully digital, for-credit learning that strengthens student retention, confidence, and career readiness. Students from all backgrounds gain early career experience, explore potential pathways, and build the skills and competencies employers expect through hands-on, work-based learning experiences aligned with workforce needs. For more information, visit Podium Education at www.podiumeducation.com and follow us on LinkedIn.

Career services teams nationwide can now use RippleMatch's career guidance, opportunities marketplace and job search analytics tools at no cost.

BOSTON, Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- RippleMatch, a leading early career recruiting platform, today announced that its university product is now available free of charge to all higher education institutions. The news follows RippleMatch's acquisition by JobGet, the fastest-growing job platform connecting workers to employers at scale, and provides universities a valuable tool to support students through an entry-level hiring market that's challenged by AI disruption.

"Career services teams are being asked to do more for students at exactly the moment when the job market has become most unpredictable for them," said Audrey Patenaude, General Manager of RippleMatch. "AI is reshaping the entry-level roles where graduates have traditionally gotten their start. The job search process has become more opaque, and universities are doing this with fewer resources than ever. With our acquisition by JobGet, we've gained access to a dramatically larger job inventory and employer network, and that growth allows us to expand access to universities at no cost, and we believe that's what this moment calls for."

The announcement comes as recent graduates face one of the toughest labor markets in years. Unemployment among recent college graduates has climbed to 5.7% — a three-year high — while underemployment sits at 41.5%. Junior-level job postings fell 7% last year even as senior-level openings grew, and AI is reshaping the career ladder.

Universities are absorbing this pressure directly. Higher education institutions shed over 9,000 positions in 2025, and budget constraints have left many career services teams trying to support more students with fewer resources.

RippleMatch's Free Platform for University Career Centers

Through RippleMatch, students gain access to a personalized job feed matched to their skills and goals, verified skill badges recognized by employers, and an application process that surfaces them directly to recruiters, resulting in interview rates 20x higher than traditional job boards.

releases.title: Graduate employability study finds career-connected learning and real-world experience are priorities for college graduates
releases.body:
Peer-reviewed article by University of Phoenix scholars identifies curriculum-career alignment, critical thinking, and experiential learning and mentorship as strategies graduates associate with career readiness.

PHOENIX, Sept. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies scholars affiliated with the Center for Educational and Instructional Technology Research (CEITR) have published a peer-reviewed study examining how higher education institutions can support graduate employability as workplace skill demands continue to change.

Published in the International Journal of Innovative Business Strategies, as the article, "Graduate Employability in a Changing World," the mixed-methods study draws on the perspectives of 380 graduates of U.S. colleges and universities and found strong agreement that employability is supported when academic learning is intentionally connected to careers, practical applications and opportunities to develop adaptable skills.

Among 11 employability strategies evaluated by respondents, connecting curriculum to careers received the highest rating, followed by teaching critical thinking and adaptability, incorporating real-world applications and encouraging internships or employment. The researchers found that graduates especially associated employability development with practices delivered through faculty instruction, advising and mentoring.

"Our findings suggest graduates value career relevance when it is built throughout the educational experience," said Rheanna Reed, DM, lead author and research fellow in the Center for Educational and Instructional Technology Research (CEITR) at University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies. "Connecting learning to careers, creating opportunities to apply knowledge and helping learners develop adaptability can make career readiness a more intentional part of higher education."

Graduates emphasize experiential learning and practical skill development

Open-ended responses reinforced the quantitative findings. Among 306 graduates responding to a question about employability best practices, experiential learning was the most frequently cited strategy, appearing in 77 responses. Other frequently identified practices included skill development, mentorship and networking, and curriculum-career alignment.

The study also identified barriers that may make employability opportunities harder to access. Among 292 respondents answering a question about challenges, time constraints and competing responsibilities were cited most frequently. Labor market and financial constraints were also identified.

The researchers conclude that higher education institutions can support employability by integrating career relevance across curricula, expanding access to experiential learning, strengthening mentoring and networking opportunities, and encouraging self-directed learning and continuous skill development.

The authors note that the study reflects graduates' self-reported perceptions and does not directly measure the effectiveness of particular institutional practices or establish causal relationships. Its cross-sectional design and panel-based sample also limit the extent to which findings can be generalized.

The authors previously presented study findings in a session titled, "Graduate career readiness and employability: Global issues in education and research," at the London International Conference on Education, November 3-5, 2025, and at the University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies' Knowledge Without Boundaries Summit in October 2025.

About the authors

The authors are affiliates of the Center for Educational and Instructional Technology Research (CEITR), housed within the University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies, which supports scholarly research and collaboration on topics related to teaching and learning, online and in-person education, educational technology strategies, and educational policies, practices and theories.

Rheanna Reed, DM, is a research fellow with the CEITR and serves as Faculty Quality Assurance Manager at the University. She has worked in higher education since 2006 and conducts research focused on instructional quality, faculty support, student success and graduate employability. She earned her Doctor of Management in Organizational Leadership from University of Phoenix.

Louise Underdahl, Ph.D. is a doctoral instructor in the University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies and a research fellow with CEITR. Her scholarship examines graduate employability, career development, mentorship, worker autonomy and human-AI collaboration. Underdahl has taught at University of Phoenix since 2004 and earned her doctorate from the University of Southern California.

Nicole Gulley, Ed.D., is a University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies alumna affiliated with CEITR. Her research interests include student retention and graduate employability, and she has contributed to University research examining nontraditional online student retention as well as employer needs, graduate skills and curriculum design.

Shawishi Haynes, Ph.D., Ed.D., serves as a University Research Methodologist in the University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies and is affiliated with CEITR. Haynes has more than 30 years of healthcare leadership experience and has been faculty at University of Phoenix since 2008, serving in multiple academic and leadership capacities. Her research interests include graduate employability, student retention, healthcare workforce challenges, and alignment between academic preparation and evolving workforce needs.

Mar Navarro, Ph.D., is a University Research Methodologist in the University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies and a CEITR research fellow. Her research focuses on cognition and cognitive ergonomics, including how people learn, understand and process information, with particular interests in online teaching and learning, student retention and graduate employability.

The full article, "Graduate Employability in a Changing World," is available in the International Journal of Innovative Business Strategies, 11(1), at https://infonomics-society.org/ijibs/published-papers/volume-11-2025/.

About the College of Doctoral Studies

University of Phoenix's College of Doctoral Studies focuses on today's challenging business and organizational needs, from addressing critical social issues to developing solutions to accelerate community building and industry growth. The College's research program is built around the Scholar, Practitioner, Leader Model which puts students in the center of the Doctoral Education Ecosystem® with experts, resources and tools to help prepare them to be a leader in their organization, industry and community. Through this program, students and researchers work with organizations to conduct research that can be applied in the workplace in real time.

About University of Phoenix 

University of Phoenix is Built for Real Life. 50 Years Strong. The University innovates to help working adults enhance their careers and develop skills in a rapidly changing world through flexible online learning, relevant courses, academic AI pillars, and skills-mapped curriculum for associate, bachelor's and master's degree programs. Active students and alumni have access to Career Services for Life® resources including career guidance and tools. For more information, visit phoenix.edu.

We are committed to welcoming new graduates and students into our workforce, where they contribute at a high level and bring new ideas and ways of working to Sargento," said Louie Gentine, third-generation Chairman and CEO of Sargento. "Being recognized by Forbes as a top employer for both new graduates and midsize companies in America is an incredible honor. It shows that the culture we have built over generations continues to drive our success and makes Sargento a place where you can start and grow your career."

releases.body:
Early College students can earn an associate degree while still in high school, potentially saving families tens of thousands of dollars.

GRAND RAPIDS, Mich., Sept. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- "I couldn't imagine how much money worth of free education my kids have received through this program."

For Ciara Selden-Ruffin, the mother of Grand River Preparatory High School Early College student Aamir Hollowell, the financial impact of the Early College program has been substantial. It has given Aamir the opportunity to earn an associate degree without the family taking on the tuition bill.

That kind of financial head start is critical for families worrying about how they will pay for college.

The nation's federal student loan portfolio stands at nearly $1.7 trillion, with about 44.6 million borrowers carrying federal education debt. The issue is back in the national spotlight as changes to the Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, Plan ended, requiring millions of borrowers to find a new way to repay their federal student loans.

For families with children approaching college, the uncertainty underscores a different question: What if students could reduce or even avoid some college debt before graduating from high school?

National Heritage Academies® (NHA®) Early College program is helping their students do exactly that.

A $67,000 Head Start

At Grand River Prep, an NHA partner-school in Grand Rapids, Mich., students can earn college credits, career credentials, and even an associate degree through the school's Early College partnership with Davenport University.

Tuition, fees, and books are covered through the program. Based on Davenport's current published undergraduate tuition rate, the value of a two-year associate degree can total approximately $67,000.

Felicia Pope, who works with Davenport University's Early College partnerships, said the program can put students in a very different financial position when they enter adulthood.

"You can be 18, 19 years old, you have an associate degree, you have the entry-level position in the field, without any student loans," Pope said.

Students can use that degree to begin working in their chosen field or continue toward a bachelor's degree with a significant amount of college coursework already completed. "You're halfway through your degree, saved a ton of time, a ton of money," Pope said.

Nine of NHA's high schools have an Early College program. During the 2024-25 school year, 565 students earned 5,186 college credits, saving an estimated $1.12 million in college tuition.

For NHA, the opportunity is about making college more accessible while preparing students for what comes next.

Koree Woodward, NHA Director of High Schools, says Early College is a natural extension of NHA's mission to prepare students for life after graduation.

"The program makes college feel more attainable for families who may not have otherwise seen it as an accessible option," Woodward said. "It helps students develop the knowledge, habits, character, and sense of responsibility needed for lifelong learning, college success, and meaningful careers."

College With a Support System

The financial savings are only part of the Early College model.

Students gradually transition into college-level work, beginning with one college course per semester during 10th grade before increasing their coursework in their junior and senior years.

Pope calls it a "soft launch into college."

Davenport advisors work directly with students on applications, degree pathways, scheduling, and course selection. Grand River Prep advisors provide another layer of support, helping students monitor grades, manage college expectations, and stay on track.

Aamir Hollowell sees that support firsthand.

"Every week, you have a meeting with your advisor to help you stay on track," she said. "They just keep checking up on you."

Grand River Prep Early College Advisor Jayme McWain said students get the independence of college without having to navigate the experience alone.

"For them to have kind of a safety net and a support system built in is a really great feature of that program," McWain said. "It creates so much more access and skill building."

From College Credit to Career

In addition to the tuition savings, students can leave high school with college experience, career opportunities, and potentially two years of college already completed.

For some students, that head start can translate directly into a career.

Grand River Prep graduate Kennah Kalele earned an associate degree in medical assisting through Early College and is now pursuing a Bachelor of Science in Nursing at Grand Valley State University.

"I don't have to take any gen eds in the college that I'm going to, and I'm even ahead in some aspects of my nursing degree," Kalele said.

Her associate degree also helped her begin gaining professional experience. Kalele works part time as a medical transport technician while continuing her education.

For McWain, the value is clear.

"Anytime you can help someone get free college when the price is off the charts, that's a great thing," she said.

And for families like Ciara Selden-Ruffin's, it offers the opportunity for her children to start their futures with a college education rather than a tuition bill.

The event fell on World Suicide Prevention Day, within National Suicide Prevention Awareness Month, timing both organizations say reflects their shared commitment to student mental health. 

The Wellness Room is part of a broader initiative between RBC and Conscientia Health that includes a wellness curriculum focused on mental health awareness, resilience, and coping strategies; educational programming workshops; and expanded support pathways for students and families. 

"This is about creating a culture where wellness is foundational to student success," said Nicole Wall, RBC Student Assistance Counselor. "We didn't choose today's date, the timing found us," said Dr. Simbiat Adighije (Dr. Sim), Founder of Conscientia Health, who has led the partnership. "But it's a reminder of why this work matters. This room is one answer to that: a place where a student can be seen and supported before things reach that point. We're proud to build that alongside Red Bank Catholic." 

The Wellness Room includes a private consultation space, a group and workshop area for peer support sessions, and a self-guided check-in tool connecting students directly with a clinician when needed. MIT Executive VP, Glen Shor, Police Chief John DiFava, and the university's negotiating committee have presented the MIT Police Association with a proposal that demonstrates a clear lack of respect for the men and women who protect the MIT community every day. The university is demanding that officers accept 0% in the first year of a proposed three‑year contract—while offering no guaranteed wage increases in years two and three.

Meanwhile, MIT's top executives received raises averaging 16.7%, more than quadruple the average cost‑of‑living increase.*  Chief DiFava has led MIT Police since 2001 and MIT must publicly disclose the Chiefs current compensation and whether he, too, is being asked to accept a 0% increase, and what increase did he receive in 2025.

MIT Police officers work around the clock to safeguard one of the world's most prestigious institutions. They respond to medical emergencies, protect students and faculty, investigate incidents, enforce the law, and routinely place themselves in challenging and dangerous situations. Their work is essential to the functioning of the campus. They also serve as a valued resource for the overall safety of those who live, work and visit Cambridge and Boston.

Yet MIT's message to its police officers during negotiations appears to be: Take zero now, and hope for something later.

This position is not only disrespectful—it is indefensible. MIT has the financial capacity to fairly compensate its police officers. The Institute's endowment reached $27.4 billion, buoyed by a 14.8% investment return in FY 2025. MIT's resources are vast; its refusal to invest in the safety personnel who protect its community is a choice.

MIT officers show up every day to protect students, faculty, staff, and visitors. They respond to crises, support students in vulnerable moments, and keep the campus safe 24/7. Offering officers a 0% raise while executives receive double‑digit increases sends a clear message about whose work MIT values—and whose it does not. The MIT community deserves better.

The MIT Police Association urges MIT leadership to return to the bargaining table with a fair and respectful offer that reflects the critical role officers play in keeping the campus safe.

The MIT Police Association represents about 42 patrol officers that work in the MIT Police Department.

PHOENIX, Sept. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix will host the next installment of its Bridging Perspectives webinar series, "Build the Network That Advances Your Career: Mentors, Peers & Community," on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026, at 11 a.m. MST. Presented by the Office of Collaborative Learning and Educational Engagement, the webinar is designed for higher education leaders, employers, nonprofit organizations, University of Phoenix faculty, staff, students, alumni, and community members. The session will explore how individuals build meaningful networks and leverage mentorship, peer relationships, and community connections to access guidance, share knowledge, and create opportunities for growth.

"Professional growth is often fueled by the connections we make along the way," said Tondra Richardson, MBA, director, Engagement Strategy & Program Development at University of Phoenix. "This conversation will highlight practical ways individuals can cultivate meaningful networks, exchange knowledge, access mentorship, and help create opportunities for themselves and others."

Exploring the Role of Networks, Mentorship and Community

Across workplaces, campuses, nonprofit organizations, and community settings, individuals are often navigating environments where formal support structures may be limited, evolving, under-resourced, or difficult to access. As a result, many turn to trusted networks including peers, mentors, employee resource groups, student organizations, alumni communities, and colleagues for guidance, support, and shared problem-solving.

The webinar will examine how these networks are built, why they matter, and how they help individuals move from isolation to connection and from uncertainty to shared learning. Panelists will discuss how mentorship, peer communities, and shared experiences can foster trust, facilitate knowledge-sharing, help individuals navigate unwritten rules, and provide access to opportunities and resources.

Panelists Share Perspectives on Connection and Shared Learning

Featured panelists include:

  • Jelisa Dallas, Student Organization Program Manager and AACE ERG Lead, University of Phoenix
  • Mari Marques-Thomas, Vice President, Impact & Belonging, Crum & Forster, and University of Phoenix alumna
  • Evener Scott, Director, Belonging, HonorHealth

Together, the panelists will share perspectives on mentorship, relationship-building, peer communities, and the role networks play in helping individuals share knowledge, gain support, build confidence, and access opportunities.

Practical Strategies for Building Supportive Networks

Rather than focusing on broad discussions of belonging, the session will explore practical approaches individuals can build within their own communities and organizations, including mentoring circles, peer check-ins, resource exchanges, leadership pathways, warm introductions, shared knowledge hubs, and community practices that do not depend on formal authority or perfect systems. Participants will leave with strategies they can use to strengthen mentorship, support, and connection within their own spheres of influence, one relationship, one resource, and one bridge at a time.

releases.title: New Survey Finds Colleges Inheriting Students With Greater Mental Health Needs
releases.body:
In new Uwill survey, high school seniors report emotional strain as colleges prepare for the touchscreen generation.

NATICK, Mass., Sept. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The next generation of college students are expected to arrive on campus with greater emotional strain and different expectations for how, when and where they receive support, according to a nationally representative survey of more than 1,000 high school and college seniors commissioned by Uwill.

Less than half of high school seniors (41%) rate their mental health as "very good" or "good." In response, twice as many high school seniors (26%) as college seniors (12%) are turning to AI to discuss relationships or emotional issues at least weekly. Among those students, 21% of high school seniors say they turn to AI because they "don't have anyone else to talk to," compared with 7% of college seniors, or because they feel AI is more supportive than their friends (11% high school, 2% undergrad).

"Colleges are inheriting a mental health crisis, as thousands of students will arrive on campus with a need for robust services," said Erin Andrew, vice president of clinical affairs at Uwill. "Students are telling us that they're feeling alone and looking for help navigating a fast-changing world. This research raises crucial questions for colleges who must serve a generation of students who never knew life without an iPhone."

Key findings include:

  • High school seniors report a decline in their mental health. About one in four (28%) high school seniors say their mental health has declined during the past three years. 
  • Students are uncertain about what comes next. Only 19% of all respondents feel very or extremely prepared for their next step. Career or job uncertainty ranks as a top stressor for 46% of college seniors. More than half of undergraduate men (55%) worry about career or job uncertainty, compared to 39% of undergraduate women. 
  • Uncertainty about the future extends to institutions. College seniors and high school seniors alike do not trust institutions within the federal government, including Congress (trusted by 7% overall), the President (6%), and the Supreme Court (10%), the news media (7%) or big tech companies (5%) to act in their best interest. Health care providers, scientists, and educational institutions ranked highest, though none were trusted by a majority of either student cohort. One in 4 of all students surveyed don't trust any of the institutions tested.
  • Financial pressure weighs heavily on students. Nearly four in ten college seniors (39%) report working more than 21 hours per week, and 39% identify financial concerns as a top stressor. 47% of first-generation college seniors said financial concerns are a top stressor.

"The public mood around technology is shifting as parents, educators, and policymakers ask harder questions about the effects of constant connectivity and social media use on mental health," said Michael London, founder and CEO of Uwill. "This survey brings those concerns into sharper focus. They must be prepared to support a generation arriving on campus with greater mental health needs and fewer trusted places to turn."

College Pulse conducted the survey in June 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 1,020 students: rising high school seniors and rising undergraduate seniors enrolled at four-year colleges and universities across the United States. Fieldwork was conducted June 17–22, 2026. The results were weighted to reflect the U.S. college and high school student population.

As the most cost-effective way to enhance a school's mental health offering, Uwill partners with 1,000+ colleges and K12 districts worldwide, including Rutgers University, Dartmouth College, University of Michigan, Northeastern University, Phillips Academy Andover, and Virginia Beach City Public Schools. releases.title: Professional Physical Therapy Launches RISE Program to Help Physical Therapists Repay Student Loans
releases.body:
New RISE Program will provide eligible participants with up to $50,000 in student loan repayment support

MELVILLE, N.Y., Sept. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Professional Physical Therapy today announced a new program designed to help current and future physical therapists overcome one of the profession's most significant barriers: student loan debt.

Through its new Student Loan Repayment Incentive Supporting Employees (RISE) Program, eligible participants can receive up to $50,000 paid toward qualifying student loans over five years of full-time employment with Professional Physical Therapy.

RISE at a Glance

  • Up to $50,000 in student loan repayment support over five years of eligible employment
  • Payments made directly to qualifying student loan servicers
  • Open to licensed physical therapists and DPT students graduating in 2026, 2027 or 2028
  • Potential career opportunities throughout Professional Physical Therapy's clinics
  • Program availability is limited.

DPT students graduating in 2026, 2027 or 2028 may apply for RISE before graduation, and currently licensed physical therapists may apply as they explore current opportunities with Professional Physical Therapy. For those applicants who meet eligibility criteria, participation begins after they are hired and begin full-time employment with Professional Physical Therapy.

RISE participants can receive payments that increase with each year of full-time employment, up to: $5,000 after the first year, $7,500 after the second, $10,000 after the third, $12,500 after the fourth and $15,000 after the fifth, a total potential benefit of up to $50,000. Payments will be made directly to participants' qualifying student loan servicers by RISE program administrator Clasp.

"At Professional Physical Therapy, we believe the growing financial pressure facing current and future physical therapists demands bold action," said Steve Schneider, Chief Executive Officer of Professional Physical Therapy. "Traditional recruiting incentives are not enough to address the realities clinicians face today. Through RISE, we are making a commitment to help relieve that burden and create a stronger, more accessible path into the profession. To date the company has committed over 6 million dollars to its existing employees through student loan repayments and we are looking to far exceed that number in the future."

"This is a long-term investment in clinicians, their careers and the future of physical therapy," Schneider continued. "We want exceptional physical therapists to know that Professional Physical Therapy understands the financial challenges they face and is prepared to invest in them in a meaningful and lasting way."

The launch of RISE comes at a pivotal moment for the physical therapy profession. Demand for skilled physical therapists continues to rise, while the cost of earning a Doctor of Physical Therapy degree can leave graduates carrying significant student loan debt. The financial burden associated with entering the profession may influence where clinicians live, which opportunities they pursue, and whether some prospective students can afford to enter the field at all.

Federal student lending reforms that took effect July 1, 2026, generally eliminated Graduate PLUS Loans for new borrowers and introduced new federal borrowing limits, significantly changing how future physical therapists may finance their education. Aspiring clinicians may now face higher out-of-pocket costs and greater reliance on private financing, creating additional barriers to entering a profession already experiencing strong demand for qualified talent.

Applicants must separately apply for an eligible full-time physical therapist position, successfully complete Professional Physical Therapy's standard application and interview process, satisfy all hiring requirements, and be selected by Professional Physical Therapy before enrolling in RISE. Scheduled payments begin after a participant completes the first full year of eligible employment.

"Student loan debt is one of the most significant financial pressures facing today's physical therapists," said Tess Michaels, CEO and Founder of Clasp. "Professional Physical Therapy's commitment translates that concern into meaningful action, with repayment support delivered directly to participants' loan servicers. RISE has the potential to make the path into, and through, the physical therapy profession more financially sustainable."

Applications are now open, and program availability is limited.

DPT students, recent DPT graduates and practicing physical therapists are encouraged to learn more, start their RISE application and explore current career opportunities at Professional Physical Therapy [https://www.professionalpt.com/careers/]. Starting a RISE application and applying for employment with Professional Physical Therapy are separate steps.

About Professional Physical Therapy

Founded in 1999, Professional Physical Therapy is a leading provider of outpatient physical, occupational and hand therapy throughout the Northeast. With more than 200 locations across New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts and New Hampshire, Professional Physical Therapy helps patients recover from injury, restore mobility and return to the activities they love. The organization is committed to delivering personalized, evidence-based care while investing in the growth and development of its clinicians. To learn more, visit professionalpt.com.

About Clasp

Clasp helps employers attract and retain clinical talent through employer-sponsored student loan repayment programs. Clasp administers repayment benefits and makes payments directly to participants' qualifying loan servicers on employers' behalf. To learn more, visit clasp.com.

A College Ranking That Doesn't Give Points for Snob Appeal

The Monthly's Guide Also Explains How to Pick a College in the Age of AI and What to Do About the College Closing Crisis

WASHINGTON, Aug. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Washington Monthly's 2026 college rankings, out today, scramble expectations about which schools are best — and its first-of-a-kind Best Colleges for Rural America ranking shows that some of higher education's biggest economic returns are happening in some of the country's most remote corners.

Other college rankings, like those by U.S. News & World Report, reward universities for their wealth, prestige, and exclusivity — ensuring that the top ranks are always dominated by the same 20 or 30 elite schools, which few students can get into, much less afford. By contrast, the Washington Monthly guide measures colleges and universities by how much they help average middle- and working-class students get ahead economically and become good citizens. Those are the outcomes most Americans — students and taxpayers — want from their investments in the higher ed system.

As a result, more than half of the top-scoring institutions on the Washington Monthly's Best Colleges for Your Tuition (and Tax) Dollars ranking are hidden gems that most students don't know about — and that in many cases outperform elite universities.

  • The University of Texas–Rio Grande Valley (#4) lands 16 spots above Yale University (#20).
  • Western Governors University (#13) is four positions above Brown University (#17).
  • The City University of New York's Hunter College (#15) sits seven places above Vanderbilt University (#22).

The Monthly's 2026 College Guide also debuts the first and only ranking that assesses colleges that do the best jobs of serving rural students and their communities. At the top college on that list, the University of West Alabama, students earn a median income of $64,122 four years after graduation, an astounding $26,581 more than they would likely have brought in had they graduated from a typical college. 

Other rankings in this issue include:

  • America's Best Colleges for Research, which shows that the universities driving innovation aren't just in blue states — and neither is the damage from the Trump administration's research cuts.
  • America's Best Hispanic-Serving Colleges, created in collaboration with the nonprofit Excelencia in Education, highlights the schools providing affordable, effective education to America's fastest-growing student population.
  • America's Best Colleges for Your Tuition (and Tax) Dollars ranking, broken down by region: Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southern, Western.

"At a moment when most Americans are laser-focused on affordability and doubtful about the value of college, the Washington Monthly's rankings are an important and timely resource," says the magazine's Editor in Chief Paul Glastris, adding "And for policymakers desperate to meet the public's demand for a better higher education system, the stories in this issue provide a useful roadmap."

The rankings are available at www.washingtonmonthly.com/2026-college-guide.

The 21st anniversary college rankings issue also includes these deep-dive feature stories:

How to Pick a College in the Age of AI 

From someone who has spent two decades running universities and the past few years studying how AI is likely to affect them, here is some advice for playing the odds. 

By Paul J. LeBlanc    

A Radically Simple Plan to Fix Higher Education

Voters couldn't be clearer in their demand for greater affordability, with college costs near the top of their list. Here's how to deliver it. 

By Kevin Carey 

After the Closures

How the tidal wave of disappearing colleges will reengineer America's class system.

By Richard Greenwald 

How Online Algorithms Rig the College Search Process

Search engines steer students with fewer resources toward schools with worse outcomes, many of them predatory for-profits. 

By Samantha Powers 

Praise for Washington Monthly's Approach

At a time when consensus is lacking on most matters, the Washington Monthly college rankings receive positive reviews from top education leaders.

Former U.S. Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona says, "Rankings should not reward colleges for the students they keep out, but those they admit and support through graduation. By doing just that, Washington Monthly's rankings are a vital resource for students, parents, and taxpayers alike."

Former U.S. Secretary of Education Arne Duncan says, "If you want to know what really counts in higher education, look at the Monthly's rankings—you'll find some welcome surprises."

Mark Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and former director of the National Center for Education Statistics, says, "I appreciate the Washington Monthly's focus on active citizenship, economic mobility, and the attention it gives to regional 'comprehensive' universities—the 'workhorses' of America's higher education that seldom get the recognition they deserve."    

The Washington Monthly is a nonprofit print and digital outlet devoted to ahead-of-the-curve coverage of politics, government, and public affairs. Its College Guide and Rankings, first published in 2005, has helped upend the conventional wisdom about what constitutes quality in higher education and received an Education Writers Association Award for data journalism.

releases.body:
The College will cover 100% of tuition, housing, food, and fees without loans for all students

BEREA, Ky., Aug. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Berea College is revolutionizing the economics of higher education through its Financial Freedom Pledge, a bold commitment that will provide every enrolled student with a fully funded degree beginning in Fall 2027. The comprehensive initiative covers 100% of tuition, housing, food, and fees without loans, allowing students to pursue their education without financial barriers.

"Every student arrives at Berea with gifts: talent, curiosity, determination, creativity, a desire to serve, and dreams for the future," said President Cheryl L. Nixon. "Our commitment is simple: when students bring us their gifts, Berea invests in their potential. The real value isn't measured in what students save. It's measured in the freedom they'll have to dream, explore, and become."

Under the initiative, Berea College will become the first college in the country to exclusively admit students with unlimited potential and limited resources while providing every student with a fully funded, comprehensive, no-loan degree. Rooted in access, affordability, and opportunity, the Financial Freedom Pledge builds upon Berea's longstanding mission by ensuring talent—not income—determines opportunity.

"At a time when many are questioning the value of higher education, we are reimagining our public good by investing even more resources and supports to ensure Berea students enroll, persist, graduate, and thrive," noted President Nixon. "I want to thank the College's visionary board for supporting an initiative that focuses on our mission and our students' success."

The announcement represents the next chapter in Berea's legacy of bold ideas. In 1892, Berea College stopped charging tuition, ensuring students would not be held back from their educational dreams because of cost. As the nation's oldest continuously tuition-free college, Berea is now expanding that commitment to fund tuition, housing, food, and fees for every student.

President Nixon shared, "At Berea, higher education is not about economics—it is about experiences. It is not about term bills—it is about transformation. It is not about costs—it is about community. It is about our enduring commitment to every student and the future they imagine for themselves."

The Financial Freedom Pledge is built on four core ideas:

  • 100% Fully Funded Degree — Berea funds tuition, housing, food, and fees.
  • 100% Full Scholarship Package — Berea funding, federal and state grants, and other scholarships combine to cover the cost of attendance without loans.
  • 100% of Students Through Graduation — If we admit you, we fully fund you for all four years.
  • 100% Financial Freedom — The greatest value isn't what students save; it's what they're free to become.

In addition to covering direct educational costs, Berea supports students with books and supplies, its nationally recognized Work College Program, a free laptop, funded internships, study-away opportunities, professional clothing support, conference funding, and wellness resources—creating a comprehensive investment in every student's success.

The Financial Freedom Pledge currently represents an estimated value of more than $285,000 over four years. Unlike traditional financial aid models that often leave students navigating loans and financial uncertainty, Berea's approach provides clarity, confidence, and opportunity from day one.

"At Berea, we don't just award financial aid—we offer financial freedom," said Luke Hodson, Senior Associate Vice President of Admissions and Financial Aid. "Students are free to choose a major because they love it, free to focus on learning instead of debt, free to pursue internships, research, leadership, service, and graduate study, and free to dream boldly about their future."

"You don't have to pay us," stated President Nixon. "You just have to pay it forward."

Free to Dream. Driven to Do.

About Berea College

Founded in 1855, Berea College was the first interracial and coeducational college in the South. Berea exclusively admits students from limited economic resources and provides every enrolled student with an exceptional liberal arts education, a distinctive Work College experience, and the opportunity to graduate prepared for lives of purpose, leadership, and service.

Recognized. Respected. Remarkable. Current Rankings and National Recognitions

  • Social Mobility and Public Service: #1 Best College for Tuition and Tax Dollars, based on social mobility and public service (Washington Monthly, 2025)
  • Affordability: #1 Best Value College and #1 Least Educational Debt College (U.S. News & World Report, 2026)
  • Access: #1 on College Access Index (New York Times, 2023)
  • Career Preparation: Recognized by Forbes Magazine as one of "15 Top Colleges for Launching Your Career" (2025)
  • Transformative Teaching: Nationally recognized excellence in student-centered teaching, #1 in Service Learning, #3 in Most Innovative Schools, #7 in Internships, and #8 in First-Year Experiences (U.S. News & World Report, 2026).
  • Overall Excellence: One of only 40 five-star colleges in the country—and the only five-star college in Kentucky—based on graduation rates, cost of attendance, and alumni salaries. (Money Magazine, 2025).

She earned the License in Theology from Boston College in 2019. She began her academic career with a Bachelor's degree in History from Penn State University in 1977.

Dr. Iozzio remains actively engaged in several leading professional organizations, including the American Academy of Religion, the Catholic Theological Society of America, and the Society of Christian Ethics. Through these affiliations, she continues to contribute to scholarly dialogue and the advancement of theological research.

Her work has been recognized with numerous honors, including the Distinguished Worldwide Humanitarian Award in 2026, the Eagle Publication Essay Award in 2025, and recognition among the Top 500 Most Influential Professionals in 2025. She also participated in the Boston College delegation to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change at COP26 in 2021, reflecting her engagement with global ethical and environmental issues.

Looking ahead, Dr. Iozzio plans to continue her work as a professor while expanding into consulting within theology, ethics, and academic advisory services. Guided by a philosophy rooted in advancing ethical understanding and meaningful scholarship, she remains committed to contributing to both academic communities and broader societal conversations through education and research.

The Summit brought together school administrators, law enforcement leaders, behavioral health professionals, government officials, and community stakeholders focused on strengthening school safety. Throughout the event, conversations reinforced the need for comprehensive safety strategies that connect people, processes, and technology to help schools prepare for and respond to incidents of all types.

That message took center stage during, "Secure Schools, Stronger Futures: A Strategic Approach to Campus Safety," featuring Dr. Larry Hausner, CENTEGIX and Darcy Weisner, Executive Director, Paradise Schools in Surprise, Arizona. The session explored how education leaders can strengthen campus safety while supporting the people at the center of every school community.

Key Takeaways from Arizona School Safety Leaders

One of the strongest themes emerging from the Summit was the importance of moving beyond isolated security tools toward connected safety ecosystems that can accelerate awareness and response.

Discussions emphasized the need for technology that connects existing safety protocols and empowers school personnel, administrators, and first responders when every second matters.

CENTEGIX demonstrated how its comprehensive Safety Platform® is supporting that approach, with innovations such as a new alert-activated video integrations with Rhombus. When an alert is activated, nearby video streams can automatically surface, giving responders immediate visual context without requiring them to search through separate systems.

Additional takeaways reinforced that:

  • School safety must be comprehensive. Effective strategies address everyday incidents, medical emergencies, behavioral events, and campus-wide threats.
  • People need a simple way to get help. Safety technology is most effective when staff can quickly activate it wherever an incident occurs.
  • Situational awareness strengthens response. Location information and video can provide responders with greater context as an event unfolds.
  • Technology should connect, not complicate. Schools need solutions that work with existing infrastructure and support collaboration across the safety ecosystem.

"The conversations in Arizona demonstrated that school leaders are thinking beyond individual security products," said Dr. Hausner. "They are looking at how people, technology, and response protocols can work together so that when someone needs help, the right people have the information they need to respond quickly."

"CENTEGIX is always enhancing and improving their solution and providing awesome support," shared Weisner.

Building Stronger Futures Through Safer Schools

Conversations reinforced a shared takeaway: creating safer schools requires collaboration across the entire community and technology that helps people act quickly when help is needed.

Archer Student Lending, a non-profit educational loan lender, brings flexible repayment plans and competitive rates to thousands of borrowers looking to lower their monthly payments.

AUSTIN, Texas, Aug. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Archer Student Lending, a non-profit educational lender has launched its new student loan refinancing options in Texas. Now, qualified borrowers Texas residents can easily apply online to refinance both federal and private student loans, potentially lowering their interest rates, reducing monthly payments, or shortening their loan terms. 

As borrowers continue to navigate an ever-evolving student loan landscape, this strategic expansion aims to provide immediate financial relief to college graduates navigating high-interest debt. With this launch, Texas residents will gain access to Archer's flexible repayment terms and competitive interest rates.

"Our goal has always been to help students and families responsibly finance education while providing flexibility and control of their financial futures," said Trey Simon, President and Chief Executive Officer. "This expansion into Texas allows us to meet the growing demand for affordable repayment options. We're excited to bring these offerings to new communities, helping borrowers save money."

  • Fixed interest rate refinance rates as low as 4.25%
  • Monthly payments designed to fit real budgets
  • Flexible repayment terms
  • No origination fees
  • Access to tools, support, and free, personalized counseling

"We know that for many borrowers, student loan debt can represent a substantial barrier to purchasing a home, saving for retirement, or prioritizing financial stability," said Ray Jones, Chief Product Officer. "By offering a straightforward, transparent refinance alternative, we're providing borrowers with an essential tool to pay down debt and achieve long-term financial stability."    

Archer (DBA Archer Student Lending) is a new venture launched by South Carolina Student Loan Corporation (SCSLC), a non-profit student lender with over 53 years of experience. releases.body:
LINCOLN, Neb., Aug. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nelnet Campus Commerce, a division of Nelnet, Inc. (NYSE: NNI), announced a new integration with PayPal, marking the first time institutions on the Nelnet Campus Commerce platform can offer PayPal and Venmo as tuition payment options to students and families.

The integration marks a significant step forward in modernizing the student financial experience, giving colleges and universities the ability to offer trusted digital wallet payment options to millions of students and families who already use them in their daily lives.

Beginning August 19, 2026, Nelnet Campus Commerce will roll out PayPal and Venmo capabilities through a phased implementation approach that aligns with institutional payment environments, platform readiness, and security standards across higher education.

"Students expect the same flexibility and convenience in paying for college that they experience everywhere else," said Jackie Strohbehn, President of Nelnet Campus Commerce. "By partnering with PayPal, we're helping institutions meet those expectations while continuing to deliver secure transactions, reliability, and operational consistency campuses require."

PayPal serves hundreds of millions of active accounts around the globe, with operations in more than 200 markets. Venmo, PayPal's peer-to-peer payment platform, counts 100 million active U.S. consumer accounts, with over half of its users identifying as Gen Z or millennials, demographics that increasingly shape expectations around digital payment experiences. PayPal and Venmo are already how many students and families manage payments day to day. They pay for groceries, split rent, earn rewards, and send money to friends and family. That familiarity and convenience now extend to tuition.

"Nelnet Campus Commerce reaches millions of students every year, and this is the first time they'll be able to pay tuition with PayPal or Venmo," said Frank Keller, President, Checkout Solutions & PayPal. "Families already use PayPal and Venmo for rent, groceries, and everyday spending. Now they have the option to use their preferred digital wallet with simplicity, trust, and convenience for a major payment like tuition."

The launch reflects broader shifts in consumer payment behavior as digital wallets become increasingly central to how younger generations manage and move money, make purchases, and transact with choice and flexibility. Through this integration, Nelnet Campus Commerce and PayPal bring those payment experiences to colleges and universities.

About Nelnet Campus Commerce

Nelnet Campus Commerce delivers unlimited payment opportunities for over 1,000 colleges and universities and serves over 8 million students across the United States. Using the latest technology to create unique and integrated payment experiences, Nelnet Campus Commerce solutions are PCI Level 1 validated and integrated with every major enterprise resource planning (ERP) system. From payment processing and disbursements to tuition payment plans and online storefronts, Nelnet Campus Commerce helps process every payment on campus.

Creating innovative experiences that make moving money, selling, and shopping simple, personalized, and secure, PayPal empowers consumers and businesses in approximately 200 markets to join and thrive in the global economy. releases.body:
TORONTO, Aug. 18, 2026 /CNW/ -- Anderson College and Columbia Southern University (CSU) have entered into a new articulation and pathway agreement that expands educational opportunities for Anderson graduates by creating streamlined pathways into Columbia Southern University's online bachelor's and graduate degree programs.

The agreement establishes a collaborative framework that recognizes prior learning, facilitates transfer credit, and provides eligible Anderson graduates, employees, and their immediate families with access to Columbia Southern University's Learning Partner benefits, including a 10 percent tuition discount. Together, the two institutions are creating flexible opportunities for lifelong learning while helping graduates grow professionally through higher education.

The pathway initially includes transfer credit opportunities for graduates of Anderson College's Cardiology Technology, Diagnostic Medical Sonography, Medical Laboratory Technology-Hybrid, Occupational Health and Safety and Intra Oral Level I & II Dental Assistant programs. Coursework within these programs will be evaluated toward a variety of Columbia Southern University undergraduate degree programs, including the Bachelor of Science in Healthcare Administration, Bachelor of Science in Emergency Medical Services Administration, and Bachelor of Science in Business Administration. Additional Anderson College programs may be evaluated for transfer opportunities as the partnership continues to grow.

"Strong academic partnerships create opportunities for students to move forward with confidence and purpose," said Janell Gibson, Ph.D., Provost and Chief Academic Officer of Columbia Southern University. "Our collaboration with Anderson College of Health, Business & Technology strengthens the pathway between institutions, helping students build upon their education, pursue their professional goals, and achieve continued academic success."

"Our job is to help students succeed--not just while they're at Anderson, but long after they graduate," said Rose Elia, Chief Operating Officer of Anderson College. "This partnership gives our graduates another opportunity to continue learning whenever the time is right for them. It's about making sure they have choices and know we'll continue cheering them on as they grow in their careers."

"This agreement is meaningful because it recognizes the learning our students have already completed," said Cheryl Russell-Julien, Director of Academics and Quality Assurance at Anderson College. "Students should not have to start from the beginning when they have already built strong knowledge and skills. This pathway helps them take the next step with confidence, while still protecting the quality and expectations of the credential they are working toward."

"For me, this partnership is about creating more possibilities for our students," said Heather Yang, President and Chief Executive Officer of Anderson College. "So many students come to Anderson because they want a better career and a better life for themselves and their families. Graduation is an important milestone, but it doesn't have to be the end of their learning. Through this pathway with Columbia Southern University, our graduates will have another opportunity to continue their education, open new doors, and build the careers they have been working so hard toward."

Through the agreement, prospective students will have access to a dedicated Columbia Southern University partner portal outlining transfer opportunities and degree options. Eligible participants will also benefit from CSU's flexible online learning model, complimentary evaluations of prior education and training, digital textbooks provided at no additional cost, and multiple course scheduling options designed to accommodate working professionals.

For more information about Anderson College and its programs, visit www.andersoncollege.com.

For more information about Columbia Southern University, visit www.columbiasouthern.edu.

About Columbia Southern University

Columbia Southern University is an accredited online university based in Orange Beach, Alabama, offering associate, bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degree programs across a wide range of disciplines. Through flexible online delivery and a commitment to serving working professionals, CSU provides accessible educational opportunities designed to support lifelong learning.

Anderson College is one of Canada's oldest colleges, having opened its first location in 1885. Anderson has trained more than 150,000 students over its 140-plus-year history and continues to be an empowering partner for students overcoming career challenges and transitioning to the next phase of their lives. During the past decade, AbbVie has invested more than $6 million through the scholarship, helping more than 350 students across the U.S. pursue higher education.

Renewable awards increase impact

Last year, the scholarship evolved to offer larger, renewable awards of up to $20,000 per student. Once selected, recipients may renew their scholarship for up to three additional years.

As college tuition has risen nearly 37% since 2010,1 research shows college students with chronic illnesses may experience unique financial barriers2 and are at significant risk for health problems, educational disruptions and lower graduation rates.3 The AbbVie Immunology Scholarship provides sustained support as recipients work toward their educational goals while managing their health.   

"With the demands of coursework, medical care and the cost of higher education, living with an immune-mediated disease can add significant challenges to a student's academic experience," said Jag Dosanjh, senior vice president of AbbVie and president of Immunology at AbbVie. "As we celebrate the 10th anniversary of the AbbVie Immunology Scholarship, we're proud to recognize our recipients' resilience and academic excellence and help them fulfill their educational and professional aspirations."

Making a difference for postsecondary students

The 2026 class includes three new recipients and 31 renewing their scholarships.

"I am proud to stand among fellow recipients whose character, determination and accomplishments continue to inspire me," said Alessandro Ruiz, who is receiving the AbbVie Immunology Scholarship for a second year, as he works toward a bachelor's degree in business analytics and operations and supply chain management at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. "This award will significantly support my pursuit of ambitious academic goals and provide meaningful acknowledgment of the perseverance that has shaped my journey."  

The AbbVie Immunology Scholarship recognizes outstanding students pursuing associate, bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees, while living with an inflammatory disease. Recipients are chosen based on academic achievement, leadership, community involvement, essay submissions and recommendation letters.

To learn more about the scholarship and this year's recipients, visit www.AbbVieImmunologyScholarship.com.

The AbbVie Immunology Scholarship provides financial support to exceptional students living with chronic inflammatory diseases who are pursuing higher education in the United States. Recipients may renew their scholarship for up to three additional years or until they earn a bachelor's or graduate degree, whichever occurs first, provided they continue to meet eligibility requirements.

Building on deep expertise across gastroenterology, rheumatology and dermatology, and other areas of high unmet need, we continue to invest in a broad and differentiated pipeline – spanning innovative modalities, novel mechanisms of action and next-generation approaches designed to conquer the complex biology underlying immune-mediated disease.

Today, more than 1 million patients worldwide are treated with AbbVie's immunology medicines, approved in more than 175 countries across 19 immune-mediated diseases that impact adult and pediatric populations. As we work to strengthen our legacy and drive the next wave of innovation, we remain focused on delivering meaningful progress for patients and expanding access to our medicines. releases.body:
Partnerships, training, and early-intervention resources help schools create safer, more supportive learning environments

WHEATON, Ill., Aug. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Maro Health - As schools welcome students back to the classroom, the DuPage Regional Office of Education is helping districts strengthen student mental health support through training, partnerships and expanded access to early-identification tools.

"Every student deserves to enter the classroom knowing there are adults who see them, value them, and are ready to support them," said Amber Quirk, DuPage Regional Superintendent of Schools. "Learning is most effective when we care for the full range of a child's needs, which not only includes academic growth, but also emotional well-being, healthy relationships, and a sense of belonging."

A central component of this initiative is MARO, a computerized mental health screening platform that helps schools identify students who may need additional support. While comprehensive screening tools like MARO typically represent a significant expense for districts, funding secured by the DuPage ROE, in partnership with MARO and the West 40 Intermediate Service Center, allows all Area 1 schools, which covers DuPage and surrounding collar counties, to access the platform at no cost for the foreseeable future.

"Schools see students every day and are often able to recognize concerns before others do," said Paula Kennedy, Director of School Culture and Climate at the DuPage Regional Office of Education. "Providing schools with a strong screening tool, without adding a major financial burden, helps them identify needs earlier and connect students with appropriate support."

MARO also supports districts as they prepare for the Illinois State Board of Education's universal mental health screening requirement, scheduled to take effect during the 2027–2028 school year. Because the screening is computerized, schools can conduct broad student screenings more efficiently, without relying entirely on clinical staff to administer each screening manually.

To further support implementation, the DuPage ROE is offering monthly webinars, implementation guidance, parent opt-out templates, and district case studies to help schools plan for universal screening and strengthen their Multi-Tiered Systems of Support.

These efforts come as schools continue to address anxiety, depression, bullying, situational conflict, and school avoidance. Kennedy emphasized that social-emotional learning and mental health support are not separate from academics; they are essential to helping students feel safe, attend school, and remain engaged in learning.

The Regional Office is encouraging parents to contact their child's school early when concerns arise. Teachers, counselors, social workers and administrators can help families identify school-based and community resources before a concern becomes a crisis.

Kennedy said another resource for families seeking support is BEACON (Behavioral Health Care and Ongoing Navigation), a service provided by the Illinois Department of Public Health. BEACON helps families find behavioral health services tailored to their child's needs, identifying local community-based resources and state-funded programs for which the child may be eligible.

All applications were thoroughly evaluated by an independent panel of judges.

The program recognizes students across a wide range of educational pursuits, with scholarships in three categories, including the Undergraduate Scholar Awards, for those pursuing undergraduate degrees; the Graduate Scholar Awards, for those pursuing graduate degrees; and the Working and/or Single Parent's Scholar Award, for students who are working and/or single parents pursuing undergraduate, vocational/technical, or graduate degrees.
